fields.title: Devoted to Prayer
fields.subtitle: The Apostles and the First Church
fields.description: Twenty short chapters on how the first Christians prayed: waiting in the upper room, devoted to the prayers, praying under threat, Stephen praying for his killers, the church praying all night for Peter, Paul and Silas singing at midnight, the prayers of Paul's letters, the Spirit's help when we do not know what to pray, never stop praying, prayer for rulers and for the sick, and the golden bowls of Revelation.
fields.about_html:
When Jesus was taken up into heaven, His followers had no leader they could see, no buildings, no money and no plan anyone else would take seriously. They went back into Jerusalem, climbed the stairs to an upper room, and prayed. This book follows what happened next. It is Volume 3 of A Cloud of Praying Witnesses, an Ochorus series that follows the people of God at prayer from the Old Testament to the church around the world today.

Its twenty chapters move in three parts. In Jerusalem we wait with the hundred and twenty, join the first believers devoted to the prayers, pray with the church under threat, kneel with Stephen and pray through the night for Peter in prison. On the move we watch the church at Antioch fast and send out its first missionaries, find women praying by a river in Philippi, and hear Paul and Silas singing at midnight. In the letters we read the prayers Paul wrote for the churches he loved, learn how the Spirit helps our weakness, pray for rulers and for the sick, and end with John on Patmos, watching the prayers of God's people rise before the throne.

Every chapter opens with a key verse and a story, quotes voices from the past such as E. M. Bounds, Andrew Murray, Charles Spurgeon and R. A. Torrey word for word from their books in the library, and ends with three key insights, a word for today, a practice to try, a closing prayer and questions for reflection. Two appendices gather every insight by theme and every Scripture in Bible order. Scripture is quoted from the Open Word Bible (OWB), Balanced edition, which is dedicated to the public domain.

qa.question: What is Devoted to Prayer about?
qa.answer: How the first Christians prayed, from the upper room in Jerusalem to the letters of Paul, James and John: twenty short chapters on waiting for the Spirit, praying together, praying under threat, praying for enemies, rulers and the sick, praying without stopping, and the prayers of God's people rising before the throne in Revelation.

qa.question: What is A Cloud of Praying Witnesses?
qa.answer: A series of books on prayer through the whole story of the church, named for Hebrews 12:1. Volume 1 listens to the prayers of the Old Testament, Volume 2 sits with Jesus, the Teacher of Prayer, and this third volume follows the apostles and the first church. Later volumes follow the praying men and women of every century and every part of the world.

qa.question: Do I need to read the volumes in order?
qa.answer: No. Each volume stands on its own. Reading them in order follows the story from Abraham to today, but you can begin with any volume.

qa.question: How is each chapter laid out?
qa.answer: Each chapter opens with a key verse and a story, looks at what the passage shows about prayer, quotes a voice from the past, and ends with three key insights, a section called For us today, one practice to try that week, a closing prayer and questions for reflection.

qa.question: Can I read it with a small group?
qa.answer: Yes. One chapter a day takes twenty days on your own, and with a group one or two chapters a week works well. The questions at the end of every chapter are written to start a conversation.

qa.question: Which Bible translation does it use?
qa.answer: Every Scripture is quoted from the Open Word Bible (OWB), Balanced edition, a new translation from the Hebrew and Greek that is dedicated to the public domain.

fields.title: Introduction: Where We Are in the Story
fields.body_html:
“But when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, you will receive power, and you will bear witness to Me in Jerusalem, through all Judea and Samaria, and out to the farthest end of the earth.” (Acts 1:8)

Those are the last words of Jesus that Luke records before He was taken up into heaven. Then a cloud hid Him from His disciples’ sight, and they were left standing on the Mount of Olives, looking up.

What would they do now? They had no leader they could see, no buildings, no money, no plan that anyone else would have taken seriously. They were a small group of fishermen, tax collectors and women from Galilee, in a city where their Master had just been crucified.

They went back into Jerusalem, climbed the stairs to an upstairs room, and prayed.

This book is about what happened next.

Where we are in the series

This is the third volume of A Cloud of Praying Witnesses, a series that follows the people of God at prayer through the whole story of the church. The name comes from Hebrews 12:1, which pictures all the faithful who went before us as “so vast a cloud of witnesses all around us.”

Volume 1, The Prayers Jesus Learned, listened to the prayers of the Old Testament: Abraham, Moses, Hannah, David, Elijah, Daniel and the psalms. Volume 2, Jesus, Teacher of Prayer, sat with the disciples in the school of the greatest Teacher of prayer the world has ever known. It ended with Jesus at the right hand of the Father, always living to pray for us.

Now the students must pray without their Teacher in the room, and yet with Him closer than ever, by His Spirit. In this volume we watch them do it.

The world of the first church

The first Christians lived inside the Roman Empire, which stretched from Spain to Syria and from the Rhine to the deserts of North Africa. Good roads and a common language, Greek, made it possible to travel and to send letters across the whole Mediterranean world. In almost every city there was a Jewish community with its synagogue, where people already prayed to the God of Israel and read the Scriptures. That is often where the apostles began.

The first church was not a building. It met in homes: Mary’s house in Jerusalem, Lydia’s house in Philippi, rooms and courtyards in Antioch, Corinth, Ephesus and Rome. Its people were Jews and Gentiles, slaves and free, rich and poor. Most were ordinary people. When the leaders in Jerusalem saw Peter and John, “they realized these were men without formal schooling, just ordinary people,” and “they recognized that the two had been companions of Jesus” (Acts 4:13).

They faced opposition from the beginning. Some were beaten, some imprisoned, some killed. Yet the message spread from Jerusalem to Rome within a single lifetime. Luke, who wrote the book of Acts, makes clear what lay underneath it all. Again and again, before every new step, he writes that they prayed.

What we will see

This volume has twenty chapters, in three movements:

  • The church in Jerusalem (chapters 1 to 8). We wait with the hundred and twenty in the upper room, join the first believers devoted to the prayers, go with Peter and John to the temple at the hour of prayer, pray with the church under threat, see the apostles give themselves to prayer, kneel with Stephen as he dies, watch God answer a Roman soldier’s prayers, and pray through the night for Peter in prison.
  • The church on the move (chapters 9 to 11). We see the church at Antioch fast and pray and send out its first missionaries, find a group of women praying by a river in Philippi, and hear Paul and Silas singing in prison at midnight.
  • The prayers of the letters (chapters 12 to 20). We read the prayers Paul wrote for the churches he loved, learn how the Spirit helps us when we do not know what to pray, meet Epaphras wrestling in prayer, learn not to worry about anything and never to stop praying, pray for rulers, hear James on the prayer made in faith, and end with John on the island of Patmos, watching the prayers of God’s people rise before the throne.

How each chapter works

Every chapter in this series has the same shape:

  • A key verse opens the chapter, the Scripture it rests on.
  • A story sets the scene.
  • The teaching looks at what the passage shows us about prayer.
  • Voices from the past quote men and women of prayer from church history, word for word from their own books in the Ochorus library.
  • Three key insights sum up what the chapter teaches.
  • For us today brings the lesson into ordinary life, wherever in the world you live.
  • Try this gives one simple practice for the coming week.
  • A closing prayer and Questions for reflection help you respond, alone or with others.
  • Read more on Ochorus points you to classic books where you can go deeper.

At the end of the book, two appendices gather all the key insights by theme and list every Scripture quoted, in Bible order, with the chapters where it appears.

How to read this book

One chapter a day will carry you through the book in twenty days. With a small group, one or two chapters a week works well. Read with your Bible open: most of these chapters come from the book of Acts and the letters of the New Testament, and it helps to read the whole passage around each one.

The first Christians did not have church buildings, Bibles of their own or books about prayer. What they had was the Holy Spirit, the teaching of the apostles, and one another. And so they prayed. As you read their story, may their courage become yours.

fields.title: Waiting in the Upper Room
fields.body_html:
“All of these were devoted to prayer and of one mind in it. With them were the women, Mary the mother of Jesus, and His brothers.” (Acts 1:14)

For forty days after He rose from the dead, Jesus kept appearing to His friends. Luke says that “for forty days He let them see Him and told them about the kingdom of God” (Acts 1:3). He ate with them. He taught them. And at one of those meals He gave them a strange command. They were not to start preaching. They were not to go home to Galilee. They were to stay in Jerusalem and wait:

“As He shared a meal with them, He charged them not to go away from Jerusalem but to wait there for what the Father had promised: ‘the promise you heard about from Me. For John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit before many days have passed.’” (Acts 1:4-5)

Then, on the Mount of Olives, outside the city, He was lifted up before their eyes, and a cloud hid Him. They stood staring at the empty sky until two men in white asked them, “Why stand there gazing up at the sky?” (Acts 1:11).

So they walked back down the hill, about half a mile, and into the city. Luke tells us exactly where they went and who was there:

“Back in the city, they climbed to the upstairs room where they had been lodging. Peter was there, with John, James and Andrew, Philip and Thomas, Bartholomew and Matthew, James son of Alphaeus, Simon the Zealot, and Judas son of James.” (Acts 1:13)

We do not know whose house it was. Many think it was the room of the Last Supper; others think of the home of Mary, the mother of John Mark (Acts 12:12). Luke does not say. He tells us instead what they did there. They prayed.

They did not know how long they would wait. Jesus had said only “before many days.” Looking back, we know the answer came at the Jewish feast of Pentecost, a word that means “fiftieth,” because it fell fifty days after the Passover season (Leviticus 23:15-16). So the waiting lasted about ten days. But on the first morning, or the fifth, or the ninth, they did not know that. They only knew that He had promised.

A room full of unlikely people

In Volume 2 we stood at the door of this room and looked at the faces inside. Here, let us notice how different they were.

There was Peter, who had denied Jesus three times. There was Matthew, who had worked for Rome collecting taxes, and Simon the Zealot, whose name suggests that he had once belonged to the party that wanted to drive Rome out by force. There was Thomas, who had refused to believe until he touched the wounds. There were women who had followed Jesus from Galilee and given of their own money to support Him. There was Mary, His mother, who had watched Him die.

And there were “His brothers.” John says plainly, “Even His own brothers did not believe in Him” (John 7:5). Something had changed. Paul tells us that the risen Jesus “appeared to James” (1 Corinthians 15:7), and many believe this was James His brother, who later became a leader of the church in Jerusalem (Galatians 1:19). Now these brothers knelt beside the fishermen.

Soon the group grew. Luke says that “a crowd of about 120 people gathered in one place” (Acts 1:15). They had no temple, no money and no famous names. They had a promise and a room.

How they waited

Luke uses two phrases to describe them. They were “devoted to prayer,” and they were “of one mind in it.”

The word translated “devoted” means to hold on firmly and keep at something without stopping. It is the same word Luke will use again for the church after Pentecost (Acts 2:42) and for the apostles’ choice to put prayer first (Acts 6:4). This was not one prayer meeting. It was a way of spending every day. Luke’s Gospel adds that they “spent all their time in the temple, blessing God” (Luke 24:53). Their waiting was full of worship.

What did they pray for? Luke does not give us their words. But Jesus had taught them, only months before, “How much more will the Father in heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him!” (Luke 11:13). It is easy to believe they were asking for exactly that.

Andrew Murray, the South African pastor, saw in these days a pattern for the whole history of the church:

“The great work of redemption had been accomplished. The Holy Spirit had been promised by Christ “not many days hence.” He had sat down on His throne and received the Spirit from the Father. But all this was not enough. One thing more was needed: the ten days’ united continued supplication of the disciples. It was intense, continued prayer that prepared the disciples’ hearts, that opened the windows of heaven, that brought down the promised gift.”

Andrew Murray, The Ministry of Intercession

We must hold two truths together here. God had already fixed the day. The Spirit came at Pentecost because the Father had chosen that time, not because the disciples prayed for enough hours. And yet God chose to send His gift to a praying people. Their prayer did not change His calendar. It prepared their hearts to receive what He was ready to give.

The waiting also included one practical decision. Judas had betrayed Jesus and died, and the Twelve were now eleven. Peter said that someone who had been with them from the beginning must take his place, and they put forward two men, Joseph called Barsabbas and Matthias. Then they prayed:

“And they prayed, ‘Lord, You who know the hearts of all people, make plain which one of these two is Your choice to fill the place in this ministry and apostleship that Judas deserted to go to his own place.’” (Acts 1:24-25)

Then they cast lots, an old custom in Israel. Perhaps marked stones or names were shaken in a jar or a fold of cloth until one fell out. The proverb said, “The lot is tossed into the lap, but how it falls is decided by the LORD” (Proverbs 16:33). The lot fell on Matthias. It is the last time the New Testament tells of the church choosing this way. After the Spirit came, we read of them seeking God’s mind through prayer and the Spirit’s leading. But even before Pentecost, the first thing they did with a decision was to place it in God’s hands.

R. A. Torrey, the American teacher and evangelist, summed up these ten days in one sentence:

“The first great revival of Christian history had its origin on the human side in a ten-days’ prayer-meeting.”

R. A. Torrey, How to Pray

Three key insights

  1. Waiting on God is not wasted time. The disciples did not know how long they would wait, but they filled the days with prayer and praise. God’s delays are often His preparation, and prayer is how we stay ready.
  2. Prayer made one family out of very different people. A tax collector, a zealot, a denier, a doubter, women and once-unbelieving brothers were “of one mind” in prayer. People who pray together for one promise learn to belong to one another.
  3. The first church placed its first decision in God’s hands. Before they chose a new apostle, they prayed, “Lord, You who know the hearts of all people.” Prayer is where God’s people learn to want His choice more than their own.

For us today

Many of us are waiting for something. A young man in Nairobi waits for work. A mother in Manila waits for news of a son who went abroad. A village church waits for a pastor. Some believers wait in prison for a trial that never comes. It is easy to grow bitter, or to stop praying.

The upper room shows us another way to wait. The disciples held on to a promise, and they held on to one another. They did not wait alone, and they kept praying every day until the answer came.

The upper room also speaks to divided churches. If brothers who had not believed and friends who had run away could kneel side by side, believers who have hurt one another can pray together too. And notice that there was no famous preacher in the room yet. The church was born in a prayer meeting of ordinary men and women, and God still loves to work through such meetings.

Try this

This week, practice waiting with prayer.

  • Name your waiting. Write down one thing you are waiting for God to do. Then write beside it one promise of God that speaks to it.
  • Pray a little every day. Like the disciples, return to it daily, even if only for five minutes. Do not stop because nothing seems to change.
  • Wait with others. Ask one or two believers to pray with you once this week, especially someone from a different background or church.
  • Bring one decision to God. Before you decide something this week, pray as the first church did: “Lord, You know my heart and every heart. Show me Your choice.”

A closing prayer

Father, You keep every promise You make. When I must wait, keep me from giving up or growing bitter. Teach me to wait as the first disciples waited, devoted to prayer and of one mind with Your people. Join me to brothers and sisters who are not like me, and make us one family on our knees. Lord, You know the hearts of all people. Show me Your choice in the decisions before me. And as You poured out Your Spirit on the praying church in Jerusalem, fill me and Your church today. In the name of Jesus. Amen.

Questions for reflection

  • What are you waiting for God to do? How do you usually spend the time while you wait?
  • Why do you think Jesus told the disciples to wait and pray before they began to preach?
  • Who in your church or town could you pray with, even though you are very different?

  • R. A. Torrey, How to Pray, especially “The Place of Prayer Before and During Revivals”
  • E. M. Bounds, The Possibilities of Prayer, especially “The Ministry of Prayer”

fields.title: Devoted to the Prayers
fields.body_html:
“They gave themselves fully to the apostles’ teaching and to the shared life, to the breaking of bread and to the prayers.” (Acts 2:42)

The ten days of waiting ended on the morning of Pentecost.

Jerusalem was crowded for the feast. Jewish pilgrims had come from all over the Roman world and beyond. Some lived in the city; others had traveled for weeks. The believers were together in one place when the promise came:

“All at once a sound came out of heaven, like a mighty wind sweeping through, and it filled the entire house where they sat. Tongues like fire appeared to them, parting so that one came to rest on each of them. Every one of them was filled with the Holy Spirit, and they began to speak in other languages as the Spirit gave them the words to say.” (Acts 2:2-4)

A crowd came running at the noise. People from Parthia in the east, from Egypt, Rome and Arabia, and from many places between, heard these Galileans praising God in their own languages. Some were amazed. Some laughed and said they were drunk. Peter stood up and told them that it was only nine in the morning, and that this was what the prophet Joel had promised. Then he preached Jesus, crucified and risen. The words “pierced their hearts,” and they asked, “What are we to do?” (Acts 2:37). Peter told them to repent and be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. That day about three thousand people were baptized.

Now imagine the next morning. Yesterday the church was about 120 people in one house. Today it is more than three thousand, most of whom had never walked with Jesus or heard Him teach. There were no church buildings, no Bibles to hand out, no trained pastors except the Twelve. What would hold such a crowd together?

Luke answers in one sentence. They gave themselves fully to four things: the apostles’ teaching, the shared life, the breaking of bread, and the prayers. Then he describes their days:

“Day after day they went on gathering, united, in the temple; at home they broke bread, eating their food with joyful and simple hearts, praising God and well regarded by all the people. And each day the Lord brought into their company more people who were being saved.” (Acts 2:46-47)

Four things held together

The four parts of Acts 2:42 belong together, like four legs of a table.

The apostles’ teaching was what the Twelve had learned from Jesus: His words, His death and resurrection, and how the Scriptures pointed to Him. Later it was written down in the Gospels and letters of the New Testament. The shared life was their love for one another, which reached even their money and food. Luke says they sold land and goods to help anyone in need (Acts 2:45). The breaking of bread meant eating together in their homes, and many Christians believe it included the Lord’s Supper, which Jesus gave them on the night before He died.

And the fourth was prayer. Prayer was not something extra, added on when there was time. It stood beside teaching, fellowship and the Lord’s Supper as one of the things they would not let go.

John Calvin, the reformer of Geneva, read this verse and drew a lesson for every church:

“Thus we ought always to provide that no meeting of the Church is held without the word, prayer, the dispensation of the Supper, and alms.”

John Calvin, Institutes of the Christian Religion

“Alms” means gifts for the poor. Christians in different traditions arrange their worship in different ways, but almost all of them have kept these same four things, because they are here at the birth of the church.

What were “the prayers”?

Luke does not say only “prayer.” He says “the prayers.” Many scholars think this tells us something. The first believers were Jews, and they kept going to the temple “day after day.” The temple had set times of prayer each day, and in the next chapter we will find Peter and John going up “for the afternoon prayer at three o’clock” (Acts 3:1). So “the prayers” may well include those set prayers, and the psalms that every Jewish family knew.

But they also prayed in new ways. They prayed in the name of Jesus. They prayed the prayer He had taught them, “Our Father.” They prayed in their homes as they broke bread. And they prayed in many languages, because on the first day of the church the Spirit had declared the mighty deeds of God through them in the languages of the nations (Acts 2:11).

We cannot be certain of every detail. But it seems that the first church did not choose between old forms of prayer and new, free prayer from the heart. They kept both. That is worth remembering, because Christians today are sometimes quick to look down on one or the other. Some churches pray with ancient written prayers and the psalms at set hours. Others pray freely, aloud, all together. The church in Jerusalem seems to have done both.

How they kept going

Luke’s word “gave themselves fully” is the same word he used for the 120 who were “devoted to prayer” in the upper room (Acts 1:14). Pentecost was a great day, but a church cannot live on one great day. The power that came in answer to prayer was kept alive by more prayer.

E. M. Bounds, the American Methodist pastor, put it like this:

“With the disciples, Pentecost was made by prayer. With them, Pentecost was continued by giving themselves to continued prayer.”

E. M. Bounds, The Reality of Prayer

Look again at the picture in verses 46 and 47. These people were not gloomy. They ate “with joyful and simple hearts.” They were “praising God.” Their prayer was full of thanks, because God had done something wonderful among them. And while they prayed and praised, “each day the Lord brought into their company more people who were being saved.” Luke does not say that they ran a great program. He says the Lord added to them, day after day, while they kept at the prayers.

The same Bounds wrote a sentence that every poor church should hear:

“A praying Church is strong though poor in all besides. A prayerless Church is weak though rich in all besides.”

E. M. Bounds, The Reality of Prayer

Three key insights

  1. Prayer was one of the four things the first church would not let go. It stood beside the apostles’ teaching, the shared life and the breaking of bread. A church that keeps all four is built on the foundation the apostles laid.
  2. A great day of blessing must be followed by daily prayer. Pentecost came in answer to prayer, and it was continued by prayer. The first believers kept at the prayers “day after day,” not only on the day the Spirit came.
  3. The first church prayed together, in the temple and at home. They joined the set prayers of God’s people and prayed freely around their tables. Both kinds of prayer have a place in the life of a church.

For us today

Acts 2:42 is a simple test for any church, large or small. Do we hold on to the teaching of the apostles? Do we share our lives? Do we break bread together? Do we pray?

Many churches are strong in one or two of these and weak in the others. A church may have fine teaching and weak prayer. Another may have warm fellowship and little Bible. The first church gave itself to all four.

This verse is also good news for poor churches. Many believers meet under a tree in a village, in a rented room above a shop, or in an apartment where they must sing quietly so the neighbors do not hear. They have no building and no money. But they can have everything in Acts 2:42. The church in Jerusalem had nothing else.

And it is a word for the individual believer too. Perhaps you once had a great day with God: a time when you came to faith, or a meeting where you felt God very near. That day was a gift. But faith is kept alive by steady habits: the Word, fellowship, the Lord’s Table and the prayers, day after day.

Try this

This week, give yourself to “the prayers” in both old and new ways.

  • Pray an old prayer. Each morning, pray the Lord’s Prayer slowly, or a psalm such as Psalm 23. Millions of believers in every century have prayed these words.
  • Pray a new prayer. After it, speak to God in your own words about your day.
  • Pray at the table. Choose one meal this week to share with others, and pray together before and after you eat.
  • Check the four legs. Ask yourself which of the four in Acts 2:42 is weakest in your life, and take one step to strengthen it.

A closing prayer

Lord Jesus, You poured out Your Spirit on a praying church and added to it day by day. Make me devoted, as they were, to the apostles’ teaching, to the shared life, to the breaking of bread and to the prayers. Keep me from living on one great day and forgetting to pray the next. Teach me to pray with the words of Your people through the ages and with the words of my own heart. Fill Your church in every land with joyful and simple hearts, and add to us those who are being saved. Amen.

Questions for reflection

  • Which of the four things in Acts 2:42 is strongest in your church? Which is weakest?
  • Why do you think Luke says “the prayers” and not only “prayer”?
  • How can a poor church be strong? What does it need most?

Read more on Ochorus

  • E. M. Bounds, The Essentials of Prayer, especially “Concerted Prayer”
  • Dwight L. Moody, Prevailing Prayer, especially “Unity”

fields.title: The Hour of Prayer
fields.body_html:
“Peter and John were on their way up to the temple for the afternoon prayer at three o’clock.” (Acts 3:1)

It was an ordinary afternoon in Jerusalem. The great day of Pentecost was past. The city had gone back to its work, and the church had settled into the rhythm Luke described: “Day after day they went on gathering, united, in the temple” (Acts 2:46).

At three o’clock, Peter and John set out for the temple. This was one of the regular times of prayer. Every day, at this hour, people climbed the steps to the temple courts to pray. Peter and John were not going to preach or to do a miracle. They were going to pray, as they did every day.

At one of the gates sat a man they must have passed many times:

“Some people were carrying there a man who had been lame since birth. Every day they set him down by the temple gate known as the Beautiful Gate, so that he could beg from the people going in.” (Acts 3:2)

He was more than forty years old (Acts 4:22). For all those years he had never walked. Every day others carried him to the gate and set him down. It was a good place to beg, because people on their way to pray were often ready to give to the poor. He held out his hand to everyone who passed, and most of them, we can guess, did not look at his face. A coin dropped into the hand, perhaps, and then they were through the gate.

When he saw Peter and John, he asked them for money too. And then something unusual happened:

“Peter, together with John, gazed straight at him and said, ‘Look at us.’ He kept his eyes on them, hoping they would give him something.” (Acts 3:4-5)

Peter had no money to give. He said so. “I have no silver or gold, but I will give you what I do have” (Acts 3:6). In Volume 2 we looked at the words that came next, spoken in the name of Jesus. Peter took the man by the right hand and lifted him up, and at once his feet and ankles grew strong.

Then Luke gives us one of the happiest pictures in the Bible:

“He sprang up, stood, and walked about. He went with them into the temple, walking and leaping and praising God.” (Acts 3:8)

For years this man had sat outside the gate, begging from people on their way to pray. Now he went in with them. He arrived at the hour of prayer, not on someone’s shoulders, but on his own feet, praising God.

The hours of prayer

The Bible does not give a timetable of prayer, but God’s people learned early to pray at set times. David wrote, “At evening, at morning and at noon I pour out my troubles and groan aloud, and He hears me” (Psalm 55:17). In Babylon, Daniel “got down on his knees” three times a day, “just as he had always done” (Daniel 6:10).

In the temple, a lamb was offered every morning and another toward evening (Exodus 29:39). By the time of Jesus, it seems, the second offering was made in the middle of the afternoon, and many people came to pray at that hour. When the priest Zechariah went in to burn incense, “the whole crowd of people was praying outside” (Luke 1:10). The psalmist had linked the two long before: “Let my prayer stand before You like incense, my lifted hands like the offering at evening” (Psalm 141:2).

Peter and John had met the risen Christ. They had been filled with the Holy Spirit. Yet they still kept the old hours of prayer. They did not think their new life in Jesus made those times useless. If anything, they had more reason to pray.

The book of Acts shows this pattern again. Peter went up on a roof to pray “about noon” (Acts 10:9). A Roman soldier named Cornelius was praying in his house at “three in the afternoon” when an angel came to him (Acts 10:30). In Volume 4 we will see that the early Christians continued to pray at set hours long after the temple was gone.

Around AD 200, Tertullian, a teacher in North Africa, wrote about these hours. Speaking of Peter, he noted:

“The same (apostle) was going into the temple, with John, “at the ninth hour ,” when he restored the paralytic to his health.”

Tertullian, On Prayer

“The ninth hour” was the Jewish way of saying three in the afternoon, since they counted the hours from about six in the morning. Tertullian admitted that Scripture gives no command to keep these hours. But he thought they were wise, because set times “tear us out” from our business and call us back to God.

What set times are for

Set hours of prayer are like the posts a farmer puts beside a young vine. The posts are not the vine. They do not make the fruit. But they hold the vine up so that it can grow. A set time does not make prayer real. It helps us keep praying when we are busy, tired or forgetful.

William Law, an English writer of the 1700s, encouraged ordinary Christians to keep several hours of prayer through the day. He also gave this wise advice about what to do in them:

“At all the stated hours of prayer, it will be of great benefit to you to have something fixed, and something at liberty, in your devotions.”

William Law, A Serious Call to a Devout and Holy Life

“Something fixed” means words or a subject you return to each time, such as the Lord’s Prayer or a psalm. “Something at liberty” means the freedom to pray about whatever the day has brought.

And notice what happened on the way to the hour of prayer. Peter and John were not in such a hurry to pray that they could not stop for a beggar. Their prayer did not shut them off from people. It made them see people. “Look at us,” Peter said, because he himself had looked. Many had walked past that man on the way to pray. The apostles saw him.

Three key insights

  1. Set times of prayer help us keep praying. Peter and John prayed at three o’clock because it was the hour of prayer, not because they felt like it. Fixed times hold up our prayer life the way posts hold up a young vine.
  2. Praying people learn to see the people others pass by. On their way to pray, the apostles stopped and looked straight at a man most people ignored. Real prayer opens our eyes to the needs around us.
  3. We can give others only what we have first received from God. Peter had no money, but he had what Jesus had given him. Time with God fills our hands with something better than silver and gold.

For us today

Many believers around the world already know the gift of set hours. In some countries, the church bell or the call to prayer of another faith rings out across the town several times a day. Orthodox, Catholic and Anglican Christians have long prayed at set hours of the day, and many Protestant and Pentecostal believers keep a morning and evening time of prayer. A farmer in Ethiopia may stop at noon in the field. A nurse in Seoul may pray when her shift changes. A driver in Lima may pray each time he starts his bus.

You do not need a temple or a church bell. You only need to choose a time and keep it. It might be when you wake, at midday, and before you sleep. It might be at three o’clock, like Peter and John. What matters is the faithfulness, not the hour.

But do not let your hour of prayer become a wall. If someone is sitting at the gate as you go in to pray, stop. Look at them. Ask God what you have to give. Sometimes it will be money or food. Sometimes it will be time, a prayer, or a word about Jesus. The man at the gate went into the temple that day because two men on their way to pray took the time to see him.

Try this

This week, keep three hours of prayer.

  • Choose three times. Pick a morning, a midday and an evening time that fit your day, and set a reminder if you can.
  • Have something fixed. At each time, pray the Lord’s Prayer or a short psalm such as Psalm 121.
  • Have something at liberty. Then talk to God freely about what is happening that day.
  • Look on the way. As you go about your day, ask God to show you one person others are passing by. Stop for them, and pray for them by name at your next hour of prayer.

A closing prayer

Lord God, You heard Your people at morning, noon and evening, and You hear me still. Teach me to keep set times with You, not as a burden but as a gift. When I am busy, call me back to prayer. When I am on my way to pray, open my eyes to the people at the gate. I have little silver or gold, but fill my hands with what only You can give, so that others may stand up and praise You. In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth. Amen.

Questions for reflection

  • Do you have set times of prayer? What helps you keep them, and what gets in the way?
  • Why do you think Peter and John kept going to the temple at the hour of prayer, even after Pentecost?
  • Who sits “at the gate” in your town or church, waiting to be seen?

fields.title: “Sovereign Master”: Praying Under Threat
fields.body_html:
“When they finished praying, the place where they had met shook, and every one of them was filled with the Holy Spirit, and they went on proclaiming God’s word fearlessly.” (Acts 4:31)

The healing at the Beautiful Gate drew a crowd, and Peter preached to them in the temple courts. He told them that the man had been made strong by the name of Jesus, the One they had rejected and God had raised from the dead.

The temple leaders were angry. Before the day was over, the priests, the captain of the temple guard and the Sadducees came and arrested Peter and John. Because evening had come, they locked them up for the night (Acts 4:3). Yet Luke adds that many who heard the message believed, “and the count of men rose to about 5,000” (Acts 4:4).

The next morning the two fishermen stood before the most powerful men in the nation. Annas and Caiaphas were there, the same men who had questioned Jesus on the night of His arrest and sent Him on to Pilate (John 18:24-28). They asked, “What sort of power, or what sort of name, did you use to do this?” (Acts 4:7). Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, answered plainly: it was done in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, “whom you crucified and whom God raised from the dead” (Acts 4:10).

The council did not know what to do. The healed man was standing right there. And these were not trained teachers:

“The council members saw how freely Peter and John spoke, and they realized these were men without formal schooling, just ordinary people. This astonished them, and they recognized that the two had been companions of Jesus.” (Acts 4:13)

So they threatened them and ordered them never again to speak or teach in the name of Jesus. Peter and John replied, “For our part, we cannot stay silent about the things we have seen and heard” (Acts 4:20). After more threats, the council let them go.

Where did they go? Not to a lawyer, and not into hiding. “The two went back to their fellow believers and gave an account of everything the chief priests and elders had told them” (Acts 4:23). The church listened. Everyone understood what this meant. The men who had killed Jesus were now warning His followers. What would the church do?

They prayed.

The prayer they prayed

In Volume 2 we saw that they prayed together, with one voice. Here we will look closely at what they said, because Luke has kept the whole prayer for us. It is one of the longest prayers of the church in the New Testament.

They began with God, not with the danger:

“When they heard it, they lifted their voices to God together and prayed: ‘Sovereign Master, maker of heaven and earth, of the sea, and of everything they hold!’” (Acts 4:24)

The word translated “Sovereign Master” was used for the owner and master of a household, the one with full authority over it. Later in the prayer they call themselves “Your slaves” (Acts 4:29). In that world, a slave belonged to a master and served under his authority. This was the church’s answer to the threats. The council was powerful, but it was not their master. They belonged to Someone greater, the Maker of heaven, earth and sea.

Next they turned to Scripture. They prayed the words of Psalm 2, which they believed God had spoken through David:

“‘Why were the nations in an uproar, and why did the peoples scheme for nothing? The kings of the earth took up their positions, and the rulers joined forces against the Lord and against His Christ.’” (Acts 4:25-26)

Then they saw how that psalm had come true in their own city. Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the nations and the people of Israel, had gathered against Jesus. Yet even that terrible day was in God’s hand: “They carried out everything that Your power and Your purpose had already settled must take place” (Acts 4:28). The worst thing the rulers could do had become the means of the world’s salvation. If God had ruled over the cross, He could rule over a council’s threats.

Only then did they make their request:

“Now, Lord, take notice of their threats. Let Your slaves speak Your word with complete boldness, while You put out Your hand to heal, and signs and wonders are done through the name of Your holy servant Jesus.” (Acts 4:29-30)

Notice what they did not ask. They did not ask God to destroy the council. They did not even ask Him to keep them safe. They asked Him to “take notice” of the threats, and to give them boldness to keep doing the very thing they had been forbidden to do.

How God answered

The answer came at once. The place where they met shook. Everyone was filled with the Holy Spirit. And they went on speaking God’s word “fearlessly.” God gave them exactly what they had asked for.

E. M. Bounds saw a lesson here for every frightened believer:

“The fullness of the Spirit always brings boldness. The cure for fear in the face of threatenings of the enemies of the Lord is being filled with the Spirit. This gives power to speak the word of the Lord with boldness. This gives courage and drives away fear.”

E. M. Bounds, The Possibilities of Prayer

Notice too that people who had been filled with the Spirit at Pentecost were filled again. The Spirit’s help is not a gift we receive once and then store away. We may ask for it again whenever we need it.

The danger did not go away. Soon the apostles were arrested again and beaten (Acts 5:40). Stephen would be stoned (Acts 7:58-60), and later Herod would put the apostle James to death (Acts 12:2). Boldness did not mean safety. But it meant that fear no longer ruled them. When the apostles were beaten, they went away “glad” that “they had been found worthy to bear shame for the sake of the Name” (Acts 5:41).

Three key insights

  1. Begin with who God is before you speak about the danger. The church called God “Sovereign Master” and “maker of heaven and earth” before it mentioned a single threat. When we remember how great God is, our troubles take their true size.
  2. The first church asked for boldness, not for safety. They asked God to see the threats and to help them speak His word without fear. God may not remove every danger, but He gives courage to face it.
  3. Scripture gives us words when we are afraid. The believers prayed Psalm 2 and saw their trouble in the light of the cross. Praying God’s own words helps us see our lives as He sees them.

For us today

In many parts of the world today, this prayer is not an old story. Believers in parts of Asia, Africa and the Middle East are warned, arrested, beaten or driven from their homes because they follow Jesus. Many of them pray Acts 4 with deep understanding. Often their prayer is not “Take us out of this,” but “Make us faithful in it.”

If you live where Christians are free, this chapter calls you to pray for those who are not. “Keep in mind those in prison, as if you were in chains alongside them” (Hebrews 13:3). Pray for them as the church in Jerusalem prayed: for boldness, for faithfulness, and for God to stretch out His hand.

Most of us face smaller threats, but they are still real. A student is mocked for her faith. A worker is told to stay quiet about Jesus or lose his job. A new believer fears what her family will say. Fear tells us to be silent. The Jerusalem church shows us a better way. Go to God’s people. Tell them what happened. Pray together. Begin with who God is. Then ask for boldness.

Paul learned to pray this way too. Years later, writing in chains, he asked the churches, “Pray that I may speak of it boldly, as I must” (Ephesians 6:20).

Try this

This week, use the pattern of the Jerusalem church’s prayer.

  • Begin with God. Before you mention your problem, praise Him as Maker of heaven and earth. Name some of the things He has made.
  • Pray Scripture. Read Psalm 2 aloud, and ask God to show you how He rules over the rulers of the earth.
  • Bring the threats. Tell God plainly what you are afraid of, and ask Him to “take notice” of it.
  • Ask for boldness. Pray for courage to speak of Jesus, for yourself and for one persecuted believer or church you know of by name.

A closing prayer

Sovereign Master, Maker of heaven and earth, of the sea and of everything in them, You rule over every ruler and every threat. You turned the cross into salvation, and nothing that frightens me is outside Your hand. Take notice of the things that make me afraid. Do not let fear make me silent. Fill me again with Your Holy Spirit, and give me boldness to speak of Jesus. Strengthen my brothers and sisters who suffer for His name today, and stretch out Your hand to heal. Amen.

Questions for reflection

  • When you are afraid, do you usually begin your prayer with the problem or with God? What difference might it make?
  • Why do you think the church asked for boldness instead of safety?
  • Which believers who are suffering for Jesus could you pray for regularly?

  • Dwight L. Moody, Prevailing Prayer, especially “Adoration”

fields.title: Holding Fast to Prayer
fields.body_html:
“As for us, we will hold fast to prayer and to the service of the word.” (Acts 6:4)

The church in Jerusalem kept growing. First there were 120, then three thousand. Soon the count of men alone rose to about five thousand (Acts 4:4). With growth came new problems.

Every day the church gave out food to widows who had no one to support them. In that world there were no pensions and no government help. A widow usually depended on her sons or her husband’s family. If she had none, she could go hungry. So the church fed them, day after day.

But the church was made of two kinds of Jewish believers. Some had grown up in the land of Israel and spoke Hebrew or Aramaic, the language of Jesus. Others had grown up in Greek-speaking cities around the Mediterranean and had later come to live in Jerusalem. They spoke Greek. Many think that some had come to spend their last years near the temple, far from their families. Now a complaint went up:

“In those days, while the number of disciples kept growing, the Greek-speaking believers began to grumble against those who spoke Hebrew. Their widows, they said, were being passed over when food was given out each day.” (Acts 6:1)

This was dangerous. It was not only about food. It was about whether two groups, with two languages and two cultures, could truly be one church. It could have split the young church in two.

The Twelve called the whole company of believers together. They did not ignore the complaint, and they did not try to solve it all themselves:

“So the Twelve called the whole company of the disciples together and said, ‘It is not fitting for us to leave aside the word of God in order to serve at tables. So, brothers and sisters, look among yourselves for seven men of good reputation, full of the Spirit and of wisdom, and we will put them in charge of this need.’” (Acts 6:2-3)

Then came the sentence at the center of this chapter: “As for us, we will hold fast to prayer and to the service of the word.” Older English Bibles put it, “We will give ourselves continually to prayer.”

The whole church agreed. They chose seven men: Stephen, Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, and Nicolaus, a convert from Antioch. Many have noticed that all seven have Greek names. It seems the church chose leaders from the very group that had complained, so that no widow would be overlooked again. The apostles prayed and laid their hands on them. And Luke adds: “So God’s word went on spreading” (Acts 6:7).

Why prayer came first

We must not misunderstand the apostles. They were not saying that serving tables was beneath them. Jesus had washed their feet, and He had told them that the greatest must be the servant of all. Feeding widows was holy work, so holy that the men who did it had to be “full of the Spirit and of wisdom.” Two of the seven, Stephen and Philip, became great preachers. We will meet Stephen in the next chapter.

The apostles were saying something else. God had given them a particular calling, and they could not do everything. If they spent every hour solving problems, the church would lose the two things only they had been called to give: prayer and the word.

This was an old lesson. Long before, Moses had tried to judge every quarrel in Israel by himself, from morning until evening. His father-in-law Jethro warned him, “The load is too heavy for you; you cannot carry it by yourself.” Then he told him, “Your part is to stand before God on the people’s behalf and to take their cases to God” (Exodus 18:18-19). Moses shared the work with others, and he was free to pray.

Notice also the order of the words: “prayer and the service of the word.” Prayer comes first. The apostles knew that their preaching would have no power without it.

Holding fast

The word Luke uses here, “hold fast,” is the same word he used for the 120 who were “devoted to prayer” in the upper room (Acts 1:14), and for the new believers who “gave themselves fully” to the prayers (Acts 2:42). It runs like a thread through these chapters. E. M. Bounds studied this word and explained it:

“The word in its background and root means strong, the ability to stay, and persevere steadfast, to hold fast and firm, to give constant attention to.”

E. M. Bounds, The Possibilities of Prayer

To “hold fast” to prayer means to keep holding on when other things pull at us. It is not a feeling. It is a decision, made again and again.

Bounds also wrote about how hard the apostles worked at it:

“These holy apostles did not vainly fancy that they had met their high and solemn duties by delivering faithfully God’s word, but their preaching was made to stick and tell by the ardor and insistence of their praying. Apostolic praying was as taxing, toilsome, and imperative as apostolic preaching.”

E. M. Bounds, Power Through Prayer

“Taxing” and “toilsome” mean that prayer is tiring, hard work. The apostles did not treat prayer as rest after the real work. They treated it as part of the real work.

Three key insights

  1. Prayer is real work, and it needs protected time. The apostles guarded their time for prayer as carefully as their time for preaching. If we do not protect a time to pray, other things will fill it.
  2. Good work can crowd out prayer as easily as bad work. The danger to the apostles was not sin but the urgent, holy need of feeding widows. Often what pushes prayer aside is something good that is not ours to carry alone.
  3. When God’s people share the load, their leaders are free to pray for them. The whole church chose the seven so that the apostles could pray and teach. Every believer can help free others for prayer, and can pray for those who lead.

For us today

Many pastors around the world are in the same danger the apostles faced. A pastor in a rural church in Africa or Asia may also be a farmer or a teacher. He visits the sick, buries the dead, settles family quarrels, fixes the roof and answers the phone at night. A pastor’s wife in a busy city may carry just as much. Few people mean to push prayer out of a leader’s life. It simply gets crowded out.

Bounds described how this happens, step by step:

“The process of hindering prayer by crowding out is simple and goes by advancing stages. First, prayer is hurried through. Unrest and agitation, fatal to all devout exercises, come in. Then the time is shortened, relish for the exercise palls. Then it is crowded into a corner and depends on the fragments of time for its exercise.”

E. M. Bounds, Purpose in Prayer

“Relish for the exercise palls” means that we lose our appetite for it. Does that describe your life? It is not only true of pastors. A mother with small children, a student with exams, a worker with two jobs: all of us have “tables” that can crowd out prayer.

This passage asks two things of ordinary believers. First, help your leaders. Offer to carry some of the “tables” in your church, so that those who teach have time to pray. And pray for them. Paul asked again and again, “Pray for us” (2 Thessalonians 3:1).

Second, look at your own life. What good thing has crowded out your prayer? Perhaps someone else could do part of it. Perhaps it can wait. The apostles did not stop caring for the widows. They found a way to care for them and still pray.

Try this

This week, protect a time for prayer.

  • Find the crowding. Write down what usually pushes prayer out of your day. Notice which of those things are good things.
  • Share one table. Ask someone to help with one task, or say no to one thing, so that you have time to pray.
  • Guard one time. Choose a time each day this week and treat it as an appointment you will not move.
  • Pray for a leader. Pray every day for your pastor or another Christian leader by name. Ask how you can help carry their load.

A closing prayer

Lord Jesus, You washed Your disciples’ feet, and You also rose early to pray. Teach me to serve as You served and to pray as You prayed. Show me the good things that have crowded out my prayer, and give me wisdom to set them in their place. Help me to hold fast to prayer and to Your word. Bless the leaders of Your church in every land. Give them helpers full of the Spirit and of wisdom, and keep them on their knees. Amen.

Questions for reflection

  • What good things most often crowd out your prayer?
  • Why do you think the apostles put “prayer” before “the service of the word”?
  • How could you help free your pastor or another leader to pray?

  • E. M. Bounds, Purpose in Prayer, especially “Prayerless Praying”

fields.title: “Do Not Charge Them with This Sin”
fields.body_html:
“Then he sank to his knees and cried out in a loud voice, ‘Lord, do not charge them with this sin.’ With these words he fell asleep.” (Acts 7:60)

Stephen was not an apostle. He was one of seven men chosen to make sure that the widows of the Jerusalem church received their daily food fairly. Luke describes him as “a man full of faith and the Holy Spirit” (Acts 6:5). He served at tables, and he also spoke about Jesus with such wisdom that no one could answer him.

So his enemies found another way. They quietly got some men to say that Stephen had spoken against Moses, against God and against the temple. They seized him and brought him before the council, the same court that had condemned Jesus only a few years before. Everyone in the room stared at him, “and they saw that his face looked like an angel’s” (Acts 6:15).

The high priest asked him, “Are these charges true?” (Acts 7:1). Stephen answered with a long speech, the longest in the book of Acts. He told the story of Israel from Abraham to Solomon. Again and again, he showed, God had sent His servants, and again and again the people had pushed them away. At the end he said it plainly: you have done the same to the Righteous One.

The council was filled with rage. But Stephen was filled with something else.

“Filled with the Holy Spirit, Stephen fixed his gaze on heaven. He saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at God’s right hand. He said, ‘Look! I see the heavens opened wide, and the Son of Man standing at God’s right hand.’” (Acts 7:55-56)

That was too much for them. They shouted, covered their ears and rushed at him. They dragged him out of the city and began to throw stones at him. Stoning was a slow and terrible death. The witnesses took off their cloaks and laid them at the feet of a young man named Saul.

As the stones struck him, Stephen prayed twice. First: “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit” (Acts 7:59). Then he went down on his knees, and with the last of his strength he cried out in a loud voice, not for himself but for the men who were killing him: “Lord, do not charge them with this sin.”

Then, Luke says, “he fell asleep.”

A prayer learned at the cross

In Volume 2 we heard Jesus pray from the cross, “Father, forgive them” (Luke 23:34), and we noticed that Stephen prayed the same way. Look at the two scenes side by side. Jesus prayed, “Father, I place My spirit in Your hands” (Luke 23:46). Stephen prayed, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” Jesus prayed for those who crucified Him. Stephen prayed for those who stoned him. Both cried out “in a loud voice.” Stephen had learned how to die by watching how his Lord died.

But notice one difference. Jesus prayed to the Father. Stephen prayed to Jesus. He had just seen Him standing at God’s right hand, alive and in glory, and he spoke to Him as the One who receives souls and forgives sins. The first Christian martyr died calling on the name of the Lord Jesus.

Notice, too, what Stephen saw. Many times the Bible says that Jesus is seated at God’s right hand. Here He is standing. No one can be sure why. Many teachers through the centuries have thought that Jesus rose to welcome His faithful witness home, or stood as a witness for him while an earthly court condemned him. Whatever the reason, Stephen was not alone. Heaven was open, and his Lord was on His feet.

Kneeling for his enemies

Stephen’s prayer for his killers was not a quiet thought. He knelt and cried out loudly. Thomas Watson, an English Puritan pastor of the 1600s, noticed this and passed on what an earlier writer had said:

“When he prayed for himself he stood, but when he came to pray for his enemies, he kneeled down, to show, says Bernard, his earnestness in prayer and how greatly he desired that God would forgive them.”

Thomas Watson, The Beatitudes

Luke does not actually tell us Stephen’s position for his first prayer, so we should hold that detail lightly. But the main point is clear from the text. Stephen put his whole body and his whole voice into asking God to forgive.

This was not weakness. It was obedience. Jesus had said, “Love your enemies, and pray for the people who persecute you” (Matthew 5:44). Stephen did exactly that, with stones flying at him. Augustine of Hippo, the great North African bishop, wrote about the scene in a sermon:

“Men were stoning Stephen, and he knelt down and said, “Lord, lay not this sin to their charge.” He loved them that were killing him; since for them also he was dying.”

Augustine of Hippo, Homilies on the First Epistle of John

The young man holding the cloaks

Luke places one man in the crowd on purpose: Saul. “Saul, for his part, gave his full approval to Stephen’s death” (Acts 8:1). Soon he was going from house to house, dragging believers off to prison.

Then, on the road to Damascus, the risen Jesus met him. The persecutor became the apostle Paul. Years later he still remembered that day: “When Stephen, Your witness, was put to death and his blood poured out, I was there myself” (Acts 22:20).

Did Stephen’s prayer have something to do with that? The Bible does not say so directly. But Christians have long believed it did. Watson again:

“Stephen prayed for his persecutors: ‘Lord, lay not this sin to their charge’ (Acts 7:60). And this prayer was effectual to some of their conversions. Augustine says that the church of God was beholden to Stephen’s prayer for all that benefit which was reaped by Paul’s ministry.”

Thomas Watson, The Beatitudes

Stephen never saw the answer. He died with the stones still falling. But God heard him.

Three key insights

  1. We learn to pray in hard times by watching how Jesus prayed. Stephen’s last words echo the words of Jesus on the cross. What we have learned from Jesus in ordinary days will be there for us in the worst day of our lives.
  2. Praying for our enemies is the clearest sign of forgiveness. It is one thing to stop wishing harm on someone. It is another to kneel and ask God to bless them. Stephen did not only let go of his anger; he pleaded for his killers.
  3. God may answer our prayers long after we are gone. Stephen died without knowing what would become of Saul. His prayer was heard all the same, and the man who held the cloaks became a missionary to the nations.

For us today

Most readers of this book will never face a crowd with stones. But many will. In many countries today, believers are beaten, imprisoned and killed for following Jesus. Again and again, those who survive tell the same story: their brothers and sisters died praying for the people who hurt them. In later volumes of this series we will meet some of them. The prayer of Stephen did not end in Jerusalem.

For others, the enemy is closer to home: a relative who cheated us, a boss who humiliated us, a neighbor who spread lies, a spouse who walked away. We may not be able to feel warm toward them. Stephen’s prayer does not ask for warm feelings. It asks God to do something: “Lord, do not charge them with this sin.” We can pray that with tears, with a shaking voice, even while the hurt is still fresh.

Paul, the man who once held the cloaks, later wrote to the Christians in Rome: “Bless the people who persecute you. Bless them, and do not curse them” (Romans 12:14). He knew from his own story what such prayer can do.

And if you have been the one who hurt others, take heart from Saul. Someone may have prayed for you when you did not deserve it. God’s mercy reached the man who approved of Stephen’s death. It can reach you too.

Try this

This week, follow Stephen’s example in a small and honest way.

  • Name one person. Think of one person who has wronged you. Write their name on a piece of paper.
  • Pray Stephen’s words. Each day, say aloud: “Lord, do not charge them with this sin.” If you cannot yet mean it fully, tell God so, and ask Him to help you mean it.
  • Ask for their good. Go one step further. Ask God to bless that person with something good: health, peace, or a meeting with Jesus.
  • Pray for the persecuted. Pray for one country where Christians suffer today, that they may be given the faith and love that Stephen was given.

A closing prayer

Lord Jesus, You stand at the right hand of God, and You saw Your servant Stephen when the stones were falling. Give me his faith, that looks up and sees You. Give me his love, that kneels and prays for those who do harm. I bring You the people who have hurt me. Do not charge them with this sin. Do for them what You did for Saul: meet them, change them and make them Your own. And when my last day comes, receive my spirit. Amen.

Questions for reflection

  • Stephen’s last words were shaped by Jesus’ words on the cross. What words of Scripture would you want to be ready on your lips in a time of great trouble?
  • Is there someone you find it hard to pray for? What makes it hard?
  • How does the story of Saul change the way you think about people who oppose the gospel today?

fields.title: Prayers That Rose Before God
fields.body_html:
“Cornelius stared at him in fear and said, ‘What is it, sir?’ The angel answered, ‘Your prayers and your gifts to the poor have risen before God, and He has remembered you.’” (Acts 10:4)

Caesarea was a Roman city on the coast of Judea. It had a fine harbor and temples to Roman gods. The Roman governor lived there, and so did his soldiers. One of them was an officer named Cornelius.

Cornelius was a centurion, a commander of about a hundred men, in a unit called the Italian Cohort. He was not a Jew. He did not belong to God’s covenant people, and by the customs of the time a devout Jew would not even enter his house. Yet Luke describes him in words that would honor any believer:

“He was a devout man who feared God, as did his whole household. He gave generously to the poor among the Jewish people and prayed to God at all times.” (Acts 10:2)

One afternoon at about three o’clock, Cornelius was praying in his house. It was the same hour of prayer at which Peter and John went up to the temple in chapter 3. This Roman soldier had learned to keep it.

Suddenly an angel stood before him and called his name. Cornelius was terrified. “What is it, sir?” he asked. The angel told him that God had heard. His prayers and his gifts had “risen before God.” Then came a simple instruction: send men to the town of Joppa, find a man named Simon Peter, who is staying with Simon the tanner by the sea, and bring him here.

Cornelius obeyed at once. He sent two servants and a devout soldier on the road south.

Now the story moves to Joppa, about thirty miles (fifty kilometers) away. The next day, around noon, while the messengers were still on the road, another man went up to pray:

“The next day, while the men were still on the road and nearing the town, Peter went up on the roof to pray. It was about noon.” (Acts 10:9)

Houses in that land had flat roofs, and people often used them as a quiet place, away from the noise of the household. On that roof, hungry and waiting for food, Peter saw a vision: a large sheet let down from heaven, full of animals that Jewish law called unclean. A voice told him to eat. Peter refused. The voice said, “What God has made clean, you must not call unholy” (Acts 10:15). This happened three times.

While Peter was still puzzling over it, the men from Cornelius stood at the gate. The Spirit told him to go with them.

Two days later Peter walked into the house of a Gentile soldier. It was full of people. Cornelius had gathered his relatives and close friends to hear what God would say. And while Peter was still preaching about Jesus, the Holy Spirit came down on all of them.

Who he was

Cornelius is one of the surprising heroes of the Bible. He was a foreigner, a soldier of an occupying army, a man outside the covenant. He did not yet know the good news about Jesus. Later, when Peter told the story in Jerusalem, he said the angel had promised that Peter “will speak words to you by which you will be saved, you and your whole household” (Acts 11:14).

So Cornelius was a seeker. He knew there was one true God. He gave to the poor. He prayed every day. And he did not yet have the full light. God saw that hungry heart and sent him the gospel.

R. A. Torrey, an American Bible teacher, drew this lesson from the story:

“The man who is sincerely seeking the truth, and obeying the truth as fast as he finds it, even though he does not yet know the truth as it is in Jesus, and so is not as yet saved, can pray so that God will hear.”

R. A. Torrey, What the Bible Teaches

God had made this promise long before: “You will seek Me and you will find Me, when you search for Me with all your heart” (Jeremiah 29:13). Cornelius sought, and God made sure he found.

Two men praying

The angel’s words to Cornelius are beautiful. His prayers had “risen before God.” The Bible often pictures prayer as incense, its smoke rising into God’s presence (Psalm 141:2), and at the end of this book we will see that picture again. Cornelius had been praying at the hour of the evening offering for years, and none of it had been lost. God had remembered every prayer.

But look at how God answered. He did not answer Cornelius alone. He answered him by speaking to another man who was praying. Peter was keeping his own hour of prayer at noon, one of the three times of day that David named in Psalm 55:17. One man prayed at three in the afternoon in Caesarea; the other prayed at noon in Joppa. God joined the two prayers together.

Andrew Murray, the South African pastor, saw this clearly:

“It is Peter praying, to whom the will of God is revealed, to whom guidance is given as to going to Cæsarea, and who is brought into contact with a praying and prepared company of hearers. No wonder that in answer to all this prayer a blessing comes beyond all expectation, and the Holy Ghost is poured out upon the Gentiles.”

Andrew Murray, The Ministry of Intercession

Peter needed that time on the roof. He had grown up believing that God’s people must keep apart from Gentiles. He could not have walked into Cornelius’s house with a free heart unless God had first changed his thinking. That change happened while he prayed. Prayer did not only bring Peter a message; it made him ready to obey it.

E. M. Bounds, the American Methodist pastor, used Cornelius as an example of a devout man, and he wrote:

“God can wonderfully use such men, for devout men are His chosen agents in carrying forward His plans. Prayer promotes the spirit of devotion, while devotion is favourable to the best praying.”

E. M. Bounds, The Essentials of Prayer

When the day was over, Peter said what he had learned: “In truth I now see that God does not favor one person over another. Instead, in every nation He accepts those who fear Him and practice righteousness” (Acts 10:34-35).

Three key insights

  1. God remembers every sincere prayer. Cornelius had prayed for years without seeing an angel. None of those prayers was wasted. They rose before God, and He remembered them all.
  2. God often answers one person’s prayer through another person’s prayer. The answer to Cornelius came through Peter on the roof. When we pray, God may be preparing someone else far away to be part of His answer.
  3. Prayer changes the one who prays. On the roof, Peter’s old ideas about who belonged to God were broken open. Prayer did not only give him guidance; it gave him a new heart for people he had kept at a distance.

For us today

Cornelius was an outsider. So, in some way, are many of us. Perhaps you grew up far from the church. Perhaps your family follows another religion, and you have been seeking God quietly, not knowing what to do. Take courage from Cornelius. God sees the seeker who prays. He knows your name and your street, as He knew the house of Simon the tanner by the sea. He is able to send you the help you need.

And perhaps you are Peter. You already know Jesus, and God is asking you to cross a line that your family, your tribe or your culture has drawn. In many lands, there are people Christians find hard to welcome: another ethnic group, a former enemy nation, migrants, people of another faith. Peter learned on a rooftop that “in every nation” God accepts those who fear Him. The gospel is for all.

Finally, keep your hours of prayer. Neither Cornelius nor Peter was waiting for a vision. They were simply keeping their daily times with God. The vision came in the middle of an ordinary habit. God still meets people that way, on a rooftop, in a kitchen, in a guard house, on a bus.

Try this

This week, practice the kind of prayer that brought Cornelius and Peter together.

  • Keep an hour. Choose a fixed time each day, as Cornelius did at three and Peter did at noon. Set a reminder and stop for five minutes of prayer.
  • Pray with your hands open. Give something to someone in need this week, and offer that gift to God along with your prayers.
  • Pray for a seeker. Think of one person you know who is searching for God. Ask the Lord to send someone to them, and ask whether that someone might be you.
  • Ask God to show you your “unclean” line. Ask Him honestly whether there is a group of people you have been unwilling to welcome. Listen, and be ready to obey.

A closing prayer

Father, You heard the prayers of a Roman soldier, and You remembered every one. Thank You that no prayer offered to You in sincerity is ever lost. Let my prayers rise before You like incense. Open my eyes, as You opened Peter’s, to see that You do not favor one person over another. Send me to the people You are preparing, and make me ready to go when You call. Bring the seekers of my city and my nation to Jesus. In His name I pray. Amen.

Questions for reflection

  • Cornelius prayed faithfully for a long time before he saw an answer. What helps you keep praying when you see nothing happening?
  • Can you remember a time when God answered your prayer through another person, or used you to answer someone else’s?
  • Is there a group of people you find it hard to welcome? What would it mean to “go without any hesitation,” as the Spirit told Peter?
