fields.title: Peter in Prison, the Church on Its Knees
fields.body_html:
“So Peter was under guard in the prison, but the church was praying to God for him without letup.” (Acts 12:5)

The story begins with a grave.

King Herod Agrippa, a grandson of the Herod who tried to kill the baby Jesus, turned violently against the church. Luke tells it in one short, terrible sentence:

“He executed James, John’s brother, with the sword.” (Acts 12:2)

James was one of the first fishermen Jesus called. He had been with Jesus on the mountain when His face shone, and in the garden when He prayed in agony. He was one of the inner three. Now he was dead, the first of the twelve apostles to die for his Lord. Luke gives him only one verse.

The killing pleased many people, so Herod went further. He arrested Peter. It was the week of the Feast of Unleavened Bread, the festival that came with the Passover, and Jerusalem was full of pilgrims. Herod planned to bring Peter out before the crowds when the feast was over. Everyone could guess what that meant. James’s death had shown it.

Herod made sure that Peter could not escape. He handed Peter over to four squads of four soldiers, sixteen men taking turns. At night Peter slept chained between two of them, with more guards at the door.

And the church? The church had no soldiers and no influence at the palace. It had just buried one of its leaders. It did the one thing it could do. “The church was praying to God for him without letup.” Day after day, and through the nights, the believers kept on asking God for Peter’s life.

On the last night, the night before the trial, the answer came. An angel stood in the cell, and light filled it. The chains fell from Peter’s hands. The iron gate into the city swung open by itself. Peter found himself alone in a dark street, free.

In Volume 2 we stood with Rhoda at the gate of Mary’s house and laughed at the joy of that night. Here we look more closely at the praying that came before the knock, and at the questions it leaves us with.

“Without letup”

The phrase Luke uses means praying with intensity, stretched out toward God. R. A. Torrey, the American Bible teacher, studied the word carefully:

“The word means literally “stretched-out-ed-ly.” It is a pictorial word, and wonderfully expressive. It represents the soul on a stretch of earnest and intense desire.”

R. A. Torrey, How to Pray

This was not a polite prayer at the end of a meeting. It was the church leaning its whole weight on God.

How long did they pray? Luke does not tell us exactly. Peter was arrested during the feast, which lasted seven days, and was held until it ended. So the church may have prayed for a week or more. At least on the last night, many of them were still awake and praying together at Mary’s house, very late.

That tells us something important. The church did not pray once and then go home. Night after night, nothing seemed to change. Peter was still in chains. The trial was coming closer. And they kept on.

What about James?

Here we must be honest. If the church prayed for Peter with such passion, did it not also pray for James? Luke does not say. But it is hard to imagine that these believers, who prayed about everything, were silent while one of the apostles sat in Herod’s prison. They loved James as much as they loved Peter.

Yet James died, and Peter walked free.

Some have tried to explain this simply: the church must have prayed for Peter but not for James, or prayed harder the second time. The Bible gives us no such explanation, and we should not invent one. It would place a heavy and unfair burden on the believers who buried James. The truth is that we do not know why God rescued one apostle and not the other.

What we do know is this. Jesus Himself had told James this would happen. Years before, James and his brother had asked for places of honor in His kingdom. Jesus answered, “The cup I drink, you will drink” (Mark 10:39). James’s death was not a mistake that God failed to stop. It was a cup he shared with his Lord.

The letter to the Hebrews describes the same mystery. Some of God’s people, by faith, “got away from the sword’s edge,” while others “were stoned, sawn in two, cut down by the sword” (Hebrews 11:34-37). Both groups were faithful. Both were loved. The difference lay in the purposes of God, not in the quality of their faith. Even Peter’s rescue was not forever. Jesus had told him that one day he too would die for Him (John 21:18-19), and the early church remembered that he did.

Thomas Watson, the English Puritan, wrote words that help us hold this:

“Those whom God intends to save from hell, he does not save from the cross.”

Thomas Watson, The Lord’s Prayer

So the church that prayed for Peter did not pray because it was sure of the answer. It prayed because it trusted the God who answers, even when His answers are hard to understand.

“You have lost your mind!”

There is one more surprise in this story. When Rhoda ran in to say that Peter was at the gate, the praying believers did not believe her. “You have lost your mind!” they said. Then, “It is his angel” (Acts 12:15). They had been asking God for this very thing, and when it came, it seemed impossible.

Perhaps James’s death had taught them to expect the worst. Perhaps their faith was tired after many nights. Whatever the reason, their prayers were stronger than their expectations. And God answered them anyway.

This should comfort us. God did not wait for the church to have perfect faith. He heard prayers offered by people who were grieving, frightened and unsure. Watson put it memorably:

“The angel fetched Peter out of prison, but it was prayer fetched the angel.”

Thomas Watson, All Things for Good

Luke ends the chapter with Herod himself. Not long afterward, as the crowds praised him as a god, he was struck down and died. Then Luke adds: “But the word of God went on growing and spreading” (Acts 12:24). The king who killed James was gone. The church that prayed was still there.

Three key insights

  1. The church’s first and strongest response to danger is prayer. The believers in Jerusalem had no power to free Peter. They did what they could do, and it turned out to be the most powerful thing of all.
  2. God’s different answers are not a measure of our faith. James died and Peter lived, and Scripture does not blame the church for either. We may pray for two people with the same love and see God answer differently. His ways are higher than ours.
  3. God answers even prayers mixed with doubt. The believers could hardly believe their prayer had been answered. God did not wait for their faith to be perfect. Our weak, tired prayers still reach Him.

For us today

Around the world today, believers are in prison for their faith. In some countries, pastors are held for years without trial. Churches in safer places can do what the church in Jerusalem did: pray earnestly, together, by name, without letup. Some of those prisoners will be released. Some will not. We pray for both, and we leave the outcome with God.

Many of us also know the pain of the “James” prayers. We prayed for a mother with cancer, and she died. We prayed for a friend, and another friend with the same illness was healed instead. It is right to bring that sorrow to God honestly. The Bible does not hide it. James gets only one verse in Acts, but he is not forgotten by God.

And some of us need the lesson of Mary’s house. We have prayed so long that we have stopped expecting anything. When God answers, we may be the last to believe it. Keep praying anyway. God hears tired prayers too.

Try this

This week, pray like the church in Jerusalem.

  • Pray for a prisoner. Learn the name of one Christian imprisoned for their faith today, and pray for them by name every day this week.
  • Pray with others. Gather two or three believers, in a home if you can, and spend time praying together for someone in serious trouble.
  • Tell God about your “James.” If there is a prayer that God answered differently than you hoped, tell Him honestly how you feel. Then ask Him for the grace to trust Him.
  • Watch for the knock. Write down what you are asking God for, and check your list each evening. Be ready to be surprised.

A closing prayer

Lord God, You saw James die, and You opened the prison for Peter. I do not understand all Your ways, but I trust You. Teach me to pray as Your church prayed in Jerusalem, with my whole heart and without letup. I pray for my brothers and sisters in prison for Your name today. Strengthen them, comfort them, and set them free if it is Your will. When my faith is tired, hear my prayers anyway, and when You answer, give me the joy to believe it. In Jesus’ name. Amen.

Questions for reflection

  • Why do you think the believers found it so hard to believe that their prayer had been answered?
  • How do you respond when God answers prayers for two people differently?
  • Who could you pray for “without letup” this week, the way the church prayed for Peter?

  • Thomas Watson, All Things for Good, especially “The best things work for good to the godly”
  • E. M. Bounds, The Possibilities of Prayer, especially “Prayer Miracles”

fields.title: Worship, Fasting and Sending
fields.body_html:
“While they were serving the Lord in worship and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, ‘Set Barnabas and Saul apart for Me, for the work I have called them to do.’ Then, after more fasting and prayer, they laid their hands on the two men and let them go.” (Acts 13:2-3)

Antioch was a great city. It stood in Syria, on a river not far from the Mediterranean Sea, and it was one of the largest cities in the Roman world. Traders and travelers from every direction passed through its streets. Greeks, Syrians, Romans and Jews lived side by side.

The church in Antioch began in an unexpected way. After Stephen was killed, many believers fled from Jerusalem. Most of them spoke about Jesus only to fellow Jews. But some of them, men from Cyprus and Cyrene, did something new in Antioch:

“When they came to Antioch, they spoke to Greek-speaking Gentiles too and announced to them the good news of the Lord Jesus. The hand of the Lord was with them, and a large number who believed turned to the Lord.” (Acts 11:20-21)

The church in Jerusalem sent Barnabas to see what was happening. Barnabas was glad, and he went to find a man he believed in: Saul, the former persecutor, now living in his home city of Tarsus. For a whole year the two of them taught the new believers. It was in Antioch that the disciples were first called “Christians” (Acts 11:26).

Now look at the leaders of this church. Luke names five:

“The church in Antioch had prophets and teachers among its members: Barnabas, Simeon known as Niger, Lucius the Cyrenian, Manaen, a childhood companion of Herod the tetrarch, and Saul.” (Acts 13:1)

Barnabas came from the island of Cyprus. Simeon was called “Niger,” a Latin word meaning “black,” and many think he came from Africa. Lucius came from Cyrene, a city in North Africa, in what is now Libya. Manaen had grown up as a companion of Herod, the ruler who had John the Baptist killed. And Saul was a strict Pharisee who had once tried to destroy the church. It was a group that no one would have put together, except God.

One day these leaders were worshiping the Lord and fasting. They were not holding a planning meeting. They were not discussing strategy. They were simply giving their attention to God. And in the middle of their worship, the Holy Spirit spoke: “Set Barnabas and Saul apart for Me.”

Luke does not tell us how the Spirit spoke. Many think it was through one of the prophets in the group. However it came, the church knew it was God’s voice. They did not rush. They fasted and prayed again. Then they laid their hands on Barnabas and Saul, and let them go.

So began the first great missionary journey. The gospel would travel to Cyprus, then to the cities of what is now Turkey, and in time across the whole Roman world.

What they were doing

The words “serving the Lord in worship” describe the worship of a whole community. These leaders were praying, praising, perhaps singing psalms and reading Scripture together. And they were fasting.

Fasting means going without food, or certain kinds of food, for a time in order to give special attention to God. It was a normal part of life for God’s people in the Bible. Jesus did not say if you fast, but “When you fast” (Matthew 6:16), and He taught His followers to do it quietly, before their Father who sees in secret.

Why fast? Andrew Murray, the South African pastor, explained it with a picture of two hands:

“Prayer is the one hand with which we grasp the invisible; fasting, the other, with which we let loose and cast away the visible.”

Andrew Murray, With Christ in the School of Prayer

When we fast, we say with our bodies what we are saying with our lips: “God, You matter more to me than my daily bread.” The hunger becomes a reminder to pray. Fasting does not earn God’s favor. It is a way of emptying our hands so that we can hold on to Him.

A word of care: not everyone can safely go without food. People who are ill, pregnant, very young or very old, or who must do hard physical work, may need to fast in other ways: giving up one meal, one kind of food, or time spent on entertainment, and giving that time to prayer instead.

How they were sent

Notice the order in this story. First came worship. Then God spoke. Then came more prayer. Then the sending.

The mission did not begin with a clever idea. It began with a praying church that was ready to listen. E. M. Bounds, the American Methodist pastor, saw this scene as a pattern:

“Here is a model for all missionary outgoings, a presage of success. Here was the Holy Spirit directing a prayerful Church obedient to the Divine leadership, and this condition of things brought forth the very largest possible results in the mission of these two men of God.”

E. M. Bounds, Prayer and Praying Men

Notice, too, that the church gave away its best. Barnabas and Saul were two of its strongest teachers. It would have been natural to keep them at home, where the church was growing. But when the Spirit spoke, the church let them go.

And Luke says something wonderful: they were “sent out by the Holy Spirit” (Acts 13:4). The church laid hands on them, and the Spirit sent them. Both were true at once. Andrew Murray put it this way:

“God in heaven would not send forth His chosen servants without the co-operation of His Church; men on earth were to have a real partnership in the work of God.”

Andrew Murray, The Ministry of Intercession

When Paul and Barnabas came back at the end of the journey, they returned to Antioch, “the place where they had first been entrusted to God’s grace” (Acts 14:26). They gathered the church and told all that God had done. The praying church heard the answer to its prayers.

Three key insights

  1. God often guides His people while they are worshiping Him. The Spirit spoke to the leaders in Antioch not while they were busy with plans, but while they were giving their attention to the Lord. Worship makes us ready to listen.
  2. Fasting is prayer with the whole person. By going without food for a time, the church at Antioch told God that nothing mattered more than hearing Him. Fasting empties our hands so that we can take hold of Him.
  3. Every believer can share in mission by praying and sending. Only two men sailed for Cyprus, but the whole church sent them. Those who pray for missionaries are partners in their work.

For us today

The church at Antioch was a mixed church in a busy city, led by people from different nations and backgrounds. In that way, it looks very much like the global church today. Many of the world’s missionaries now come from Africa, Asia and Latin America. Churches in Lagos and Seoul, in São Paulo and Manila, send workers to other nations, often with very little money but with much prayer. Antioch reminds every church, rich or poor, that the power to send does not come from wealth. It comes from God.

Perhaps your church is small. Luke names only five leaders in Antioch. Perhaps you think you have nothing to give to mission. But you can pray, and you can fast. You can lay your hands, at least in prayer, on those who go.

Perhaps God is speaking to you about going yourself: to a neighboring village, another city, or another country. Do what Antioch did. Do not rush. Worship, fast and pray, and ask others to pray with you. And if God is sending someone you love, a son or daughter, a pastor, a close friend, ask for grace to let them go.

Try this

This week, follow the pattern of Antioch.

  • Worship before you plan. Before your next decision, large or small, spend time simply praising God, without asking Him for anything first.
  • Fast once. Choose one meal this week to go without, if your health allows. Use that time to pray, and when you feel hungry, turn your hunger into prayer.
  • Adopt a missionary. Learn the name of one person serving God in another place. Pray for them each day this week, and send them a message to say so.
  • Ask God whom He is calling. Pray, “Lord, is there anyone You want to set apart from my church, or from my home?” Be ready for the answer.

A closing prayer

Holy Spirit, You spoke to Your church in Antioch while they worshiped and fasted. Teach me to give You my full attention, so that I may hear Your voice. Make my church a praying church and a sending church. Call workers from among us, and give us the grace to let them go. Bless those who serve You far from home today: keep them safe, give them joy, and open doors for the gospel. Use my prayers as part of Your great work in the world. In the name of Jesus. Amen.

Questions for reflection

  • Why do you think the Holy Spirit spoke to the leaders at Antioch while they were worshiping, rather than while they were making plans?
  • Have you ever fasted? What helped you, or what made it difficult?
  • What would it cost your church to “let go” of someone God calls?

  • Andrew Murray, With Christ in the School of Prayer, especially “The Cure of Unbelief” and “Prayer Provides Labourers”

fields.title: The Place of Prayer by the River
fields.body_html:
“On the Sabbath day we went out beyond the gate, beside a river, where we thought there might be a place of prayer. We took a seat and spoke to the women who had come together.” (Acts 16:13)

Paul did not plan to go to Philippi.

On his second missionary journey, he and his companions tried to preach in the province of Asia, in what is now western Turkey, but the Holy Spirit stopped them. They tried to go north into Bithynia, and again “the Spirit of Jesus did not permit it” (Acts 16:7). So they came down to the port of Troas, unsure where to go next. There, in the night, Paul saw a vision of a man from Macedonia, across the sea, pleading with him: “Cross over to Macedonia and help us!” (Acts 16:9).

They sailed at once. After two days they landed, and they walked inland to Philippi, an important city that was a Roman colony. Many retired Roman soldiers lived there, and the city was proud of its Roman ways. It seems there were few Jews, and Luke mentions no synagogue.

For several days the missionaries waited. Then the Sabbath came, the Jewish day of rest and worship. Paul and his friends walked out through the city gate and down to a river. They were looking for “a place of prayer.” Notice the honest words: “where we thought there might be” one. They were not sure. They went to look.

They found a small group of women. No famous preacher, no crowd, no building. Just some women who had come out of the city on the Sabbath to pray beside the water. The missionaries sat down with them and began to talk.

One of the women was named Lydia.

“A woman named Lydia was listening, a dealer in purple cloth from the city of Thyatira, who worshiped God. The Lord opened her heart to heed what Paul was saying.” (Acts 16:14)

She listened, and the Lord opened her heart. Soon she and her household were baptized. Then she turned to Paul and his friends and said, “If you are satisfied that I am faithful to the Lord, come into my home and stay.” Luke adds, with a smile we can almost hear, “And she would not take no for an answer” (Acts 16:15).

The man in Paul’s vision had been a man from Macedonia. But the first person in Macedonia whom Luke tells us believed was a woman, from Asia, the very province where Paul had been stopped from preaching.

Who she was

What do we actually know about Lydia? Very little, and we should be honest about that.

We know she came from Thyatira, a city in Asia known for its trade in dyed cloth. Later, the risen Jesus would send one of His letters in the book of Revelation to the church in that city (Revelation 2:18). We know she sold purple cloth. Purple dye was very costly in the ancient world, so this was a trade that served wealthy customers. That suggests she had some means. She had a house large enough to welcome Paul and his companions, and a “household,” which may have meant children, relatives or servants. Luke mentions no husband. Some think she was a widow; we do not know.

Even her name may be a clue rather than a name. Thyatira was in a region called Lydia, and some scholars think “Lydia” may have been what people in Philippi called her: “the woman from Lydia.” Others think it was simply her name. We cannot be sure.

We know she “worshiped God.” This phrase usually described a Gentile who believed in the God of Israel, prayed to Him and kept the Sabbath, without fully becoming a Jew. Like Cornelius in chapter 7, she was a seeker who prayed.

Of the other women at the river, we know nothing at all: not their names, not their stories. Years later Paul wrote to the church in Philippi and named two women, Euodia and Syntyche, who “fought side by side with me for the gospel” (Philippians 4:3). Were they among the women at the river that first Sabbath? It is possible, but the Bible does not say.

So we must not fill in what Luke left out. What he did tell us is enough.

What happened at the place of prayer

The first church in Macedonia began at a prayer meeting. Not a large one, and not one with a pastor. It was a few women, faithful in a city where their faith was unusual, who kept going out of the gate every Sabbath to pray.

Charles Spurgeon, the London preacher, wrote about this in his book of evening readings:

“On the Sabbath she went when prayer was wont to be made, and there prayer was heard. Never neglect the means of grace; God may bless us when we are not in his house, but we have the greater reason to hope that he will when we are in communion with his saints.”

Charles H. Spurgeon, Evening by Evening

Lydia did not know that this Sabbath would be different. She came to pray as she always had. And God met her there.

Yet Spurgeon was careful to say where the change came from:

“She did not open her own heart. Her prayers did not do it; Paul did not do it. The Lord himself must open the heart, to receive the things which make for our peace.”

Charles H. Spurgeon, Evening by Evening

Her faithfulness put her in the right place. Paul’s preaching gave her the message. But only the Lord could open her heart.

The place of prayer stayed important. Luke says that on another day, Paul and his friends were again “on our way to the place of prayer” (Acts 16:16). And when Paul and Silas were later beaten and thrown into prison, as we will see in the next chapter, the first place they went after their release was Lydia’s house, where “they saw the brothers and sisters and encouraged them” (Acts 16:40). The little group by the river had become a church, meeting in a woman’s home.

That church never forgot Paul. Years later he wrote to them: “In every prayer I offer for all of you, I always pray with joy, because from the very first day until now you have been partners with me in the gospel” (Philippians 1:4-5). The partnership had begun on that very first day, at the riverside.

Three key insights

  1. God loves to meet people at the places where they faithfully pray. Lydia came to the river as she always did, and that Sabbath God opened her heart. The habit of prayer puts us where God’s blessing can find us.
  2. A small prayer meeting can be the beginning of a great work. A few women beside a river became the church in Philippi, which supported Paul’s mission for years. We should never despise a meeting because it is small.
  3. Only the Lord can open a heart. Lydia’s prayers did not save her, and neither did Paul’s preaching. God did. That frees us to pray and to speak, and to trust Him with the result.

For us today

In many places around the world, women are the faithful core of the praying church. In villages across Africa and Asia, in the cities of Latin America, in small churches everywhere, it is often a handful of women who gather week after week to pray, while few others come. Some of them meet in a kitchen, a classroom or the front room of a small house. If that is you, take heart from Lydia and the women by the river. God sees your little meeting. He may be preparing to do something there that you cannot yet imagine.

Perhaps you live where there is no church building, or where Christians must meet quietly. The women at Philippi had no building either. They had a riverbank and an open sky. A place of prayer is wherever God’s people gather to call on Him.

And notice what Lydia did when her heart was opened. She opened her home. Her house became the meeting place for the church. Many readers have small homes, but hospitality is not measured by size. A shared meal, a mat on the floor, a room for prayer can be a gift to the whole church.

Try this

This week, look for your own “place of prayer by the river.”

  • Find your place. Choose a regular place where you will meet God, alone or with others, and go there faithfully this week, even if nothing seems special.
  • Join or start a small meeting. If there is a small prayer group near you, join it. If there is not, invite two or three others to pray with you once this week.
  • Pray for an open heart. Name one person you long to see come to Christ. Ask the Lord to open their heart, as He opened Lydia’s.
  • Open your home. Invite someone into your home this week for a meal or for prayer, as Lydia did.

A closing prayer

Lord, You saw a few women praying by a river, and You sent Your servants to find them. Thank You that no meeting is too small for You. Make me faithful in the place of prayer, week after week, whether anything seems to happen or not. Open my heart to hear Your word, and open the hearts of those I love who do not yet know You. Make my home a place where Your people are welcome. Do great things through small beginnings, for the glory of Jesus. Amen.

Questions for reflection

  • Lydia was praying faithfully before she heard about Jesus. What does her story teach you about the value of regular prayer?
  • Why do you think God chose to begin the church in Philippi at a small prayer meeting of women?
  • How could your home become a “place of prayer” for others?

fields.title: Songs at Midnight
fields.body_html:
“At midnight, as Paul and Silas prayed, they sang praises to God, and the prisoners listened.” (Acts 16:25)

The trouble began on the way to prayer.

In the last chapter we met Lydia and the women who gathered by the river outside Philippi. Paul and his friends kept going to that place of prayer. One day a slave girl began to follow them. She had a spirit that let her tell fortunes, and her owners made a lot of money from her. Day after day she walked behind them, shouting, “These men are servants of the Most High God, and they are announcing to you a way of salvation!” (Acts 16:17). What she said was true, but the spirit inside her was not from God. After many days Paul turned and spoke to the spirit in the name of Jesus Christ, and it came out of her that same hour.

Her owners did not rejoice that she was free. They saw only that their income was gone. They seized Paul and Silas, dragged them to the marketplace and accused them before the city rulers. A crowd joined the attack. Then came the punishment:

“The crowd too rose up against them, and the magistrates tore the clothes off them and ordered them beaten with rods. When they had struck them many blows, they threw them into prison and told the jailer to keep them safely locked up. Given such a charge, the jailer threw them into the inner part of the prison and made their feet fast in the stocks.” (Acts 16:22-24)

Picture that place. The inner prison was the darkest and most secure room. The stocks were heavy pieces of wood with holes for the feet, so that a prisoner could not stand or turn over. Their backs were open and bleeding from the rods. They had no trial and no idea what the morning would bring.

And at midnight, they sang.

Luke does not tell us what songs they chose. Many think they sang psalms, the prayer book and hymnbook of the Jewish people, which both men had known since childhood. But that is a guess. What Luke does tell us is this: they prayed, they sang praises to God, and the other prisoners lay in the dark and listened.

Then the ground shook. “All at once a great earthquake struck, so strong that the prison was shaken to its foundations. In that instant all the doors came open, and the chains of every prisoner fell loose” (Acts 16:26). The jailer woke, saw the open doors and drew his sword to kill himself. In that world a guard who lost his prisoners could pay with his own life (compare Acts 12:19). But Paul shouted, “Do not hurt yourself! Every one of us is still here!” (Acts 16:28). The jailer ran in, trembling, and fell at their feet. “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?” he asked. They answered, “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household” (Acts 16:30-31).

Before morning the man who had locked their feet in the stocks was washing their wounds. He and all his family were baptized. And Luke ends the night with a meal: “Leading them up into his house, he spread a table for them, and the whole household rejoiced with him, now that he had believed in God” (Acts 16:34).

Who they were

Silas is less famous than Paul, but he was no ordinary helper. He was one of the leaders of the church in Jerusalem, one of the men “who held leading places among the brothers and sisters” (Acts 15:22), and a prophet who encouraged the churches. In Paul’s letters he appears under the name Silvanus. Like Paul, he was a Roman citizen (Acts 16:37).

Philippi was a Roman colony, a city that lived by Roman law. Under that law a Roman citizen should not be beaten without a trial. When the rulers learned the next morning whom they had flogged, they were frightened and came to plead with them. But Paul and Silas do not seem to have claimed their rights as citizens when the rods came down. Luke does not say why. They suffered first, and they sang in the dark.

Paul never forgot that night. Writing to another church soon after, he said, “We had already suffered and been shamefully treated in Philippi, as you know, but our God gave us courage to tell you His gospel in spite of strong opposition” (1 Thessalonians 2:2).

How they prayed

Notice how Luke joins the two things together: “as Paul and Silas prayed, they sang praises to God.” Their prayer became a song. They did not first wait for the earthquake and then give thanks. They praised God while the doors were still locked and their feet were still in the stocks. The praise came before the answer, not after it.

This is not pretending. The pain was real, and that is what made their praise a sacrifice. The letter to the Hebrews speaks of “a sacrifice of praise at all times: the fruit of lips that give thanks to His name” (Hebrews 13:15). Praise costs little on a bright morning. At midnight, with a bleeding back, it costs a great deal. And the psalmists knew that God gives His people songs for the night: “By day the LORD sends out His loyal love, and at night His song stays with me, a prayer to the God who gives me life” (Psalm 42:8).

E. M. Bounds, the American Methodist pastor whose books on prayer we have met many times in this series, imagined Paul in that cell, his feet swollen in the stocks, and wrote:

“Paul was an adept at prayer, a lover of prayer, a wondrous devotee of prayer, who could pursue it with such joyous strains, under such conditions of despondency and despair.”

E. M. Bounds, Prayer and Praying Men

Bounds saw something else too. When the doors flew open, Paul stayed for the sake of the jailer:

“He did not go out when his chains were loosed, and the stocks fell off. His praying taught him that God had nobler purposes that night than his own individual freedom.”

E. M. Bounds, Prayer and Praying Men

The earthquake was not only a way out. It was a door into a man’s heart. Prayer had kept Paul and Silas listening to God, so that when the moment came, they thought first of the man with the sword.

Three key insights

  1. Praise can rise from the darkest place. Paul and Silas sang before anything changed. Praise in hard times is not denial of the pain; it is a choice to trust God in the middle of it.
  2. It is a gift to have someone to pray with in the dark. Paul was not alone that night. Two voices kept each other going, and together they became a witness that the whole prison heard.
  3. God’s purpose in our trouble may be bigger than our escape. The doors opened, but Paul stayed, and a family was saved. Prayer keeps our eyes open for the people God wants to reach through our hardest hours.

For us today

Many believers in our own day know the inside of a prison cell because of their faith. Some have been beaten, held for years without trial and kept far from their families. Many of them have told how they sang in their cells. The night in Philippi is still being lived.

Most of us will never sit in stocks. But all of us have midnights: a hospital bed, a lost job, an empty cooking pot, a child who does not come home, a long night when sleep will not come. In those hours it is natural to cry out, and God welcomes our cries. Perhaps Paul and Silas cried out too. But they also found something to praise: God was still God, Jesus was still Lord, and nothing that happened in that cell could change that.

Remember also who was listening. “The prisoners listened.” The people around us notice how we pray when life goes wrong. A neighbor who never comes to church may hear you singing in your kitchen on the worst day of your year. Your praise in the dark may be the first sermon they ever hear.

Years later Paul wrote to this same church in Philippi, from another prison, and said, “Rejoice in the Lord always. I will say it again: rejoice!” (Philippians 4:4). He had learned it at midnight. In Volume 4 we will meet Perpetua and Felicity, two young women in a North African prison, who learned the same lesson.

Try this

This week, practice praising God in the hard places of your life.

  • Name your midnight. Write down one situation that feels dark to you right now. Be honest with God about how it hurts.
  • Find one thing to praise. Next to it, write one true thing about God that this trouble cannot change. Thank Him for it out loud.
  • Sing a song in the night. Choose a hymn, a chorus or a psalm you know by heart. Sing it, or say it softly, when you lie down or when you wake in the night.
  • Pray with a partner. Like Paul with Silas, ask one friend to pray and praise with you, even by phone, about the thing you are facing.

A closing prayer

Lord God, You are the God who gives songs in the night. Paul and Silas praised You in a dark prison with bleeding backs, and You heard them. When my own midnight comes, teach me to pray, and then teach me to sing. Keep me honest about my pain and steady in my trust. Give me a friend to pray beside me. Open my eyes to the people who are listening, and use even my hardest hours to bring someone to Jesus. In His name I pray. Amen.

Questions for reflection

  • Why do you think Paul and Silas chose to sing instead of only asking to be set free?
  • What is a “midnight” you have faced, and what helped you to keep praying?
  • Who might be listening to the way you respond when life goes wrong?

  • E. M. Bounds, The Essentials of Prayer, especially “Prayer, Praise and Thanksgiving”
  • Charles H. Spurgeon, Mighty Power in Prayer, especially “The Power of Prayer and the Pleasure of Praise”

fields.title: That You May Know Him Better
fields.body_html:
“I mention you whenever I pray, asking the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, to give you the Spirit who brings wisdom and revelation as you come to know Him. With the eyes of your heart opened to the light, you will know what hope His call holds out to you, how rich and glorious an inheritance He has in His holy people, and how far beyond all measure is His power at work for us who believe.” (Ephesians 1:16-19)

A man who is no longer young sits in a small room, with old scars on his back and a chain on his wrist. Visitors come and go, but the prisoner himself cannot leave.

Paul calls himself “an ambassador, though in a chain” (Ephesians 6:20). We do not know for certain where he was when he wrote the letter we call Ephesians. Many think it was Rome, where Luke tells us that Paul spent “two full years” under guard, waiting for his trial (Acts 28:30). Others suggest a different prison. Either way, he was not free.

But his heart was free to travel, and it traveled to the believers in and around Ephesus, a great port city in the Roman province of Asia, in what is now western Turkey. Paul had lived there for about three years (Acts 20:31). He had taught every day in a lecture hall in the city. He had seen people who once practiced magic gather their books and burn them in public. And when he said goodbye to the church’s leaders, he “knelt down and prayed with them all. They all wept freely” (Acts 20:36-37).

Now, years later, news reached him in his chains. The believers were still standing. They trusted the Lord Jesus, and they loved all God’s people (Ephesians 1:15).

What would you pray for friends like that? Many of us would ask for their safety, their health, their jobs, their families. Those are good prayers, and Paul prayed about such things too. But here he asks for something deeper. He begins with thanks: “I have never stopped thanking God for you” (Ephesians 1:16). Then he asks God to give them the Spirit, so that they would know Him.

Not know more facts about Him. Know Him.

The prisoner who could not walk to the market prayed that his friends would walk with God with their eyes wide open.

What Paul asked for

Paul’s prayer has one great request and then three things that flow from it.

The great request is for “the Spirit who brings wisdom and revelation as you come to know Him.” We cannot know God by being clever. A person who has studied for many years and a child who cannot read both need the same help. God must show Himself to us, and He does that by His Spirit.

Then Paul speaks of “the eyes of your heart.” In the Bible the heart is not only the place of feelings. It is the center of the whole person, where we think, choose and love. Paul asks that this inner eye would be “opened to the light.” Long before, the prophet Elisha prayed for his frightened servant, “LORD, please open his eyes so that he can see” (2 Kings 6:17). The servant looked again and saw the hills full of God’s fiery army. Nothing around him had changed. His eyes had changed.

With opened eyes, Paul says, they will see three things.

The hope of His call. God has called us, and His call has a future. However hard today is, the story ends in glory.

His inheritance in His holy people. Read this slowly. Paul does not only say that we have an inheritance in God, though that is true. He says that God has an inheritance in us. We are His treasure. A poor widow in a village church, a factory worker in a crowded city, a prisoner in chains: in God’s eyes each one is part of His rich and glorious inheritance.

His power at work for us. This is no small power. It is “the working of His mighty strength, which He put to work in Christ when He raised Him from the dead and set Him at His right hand in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 1:19-20). The same power that emptied the tomb is at work for those who believe.

How Paul prayed

Andrew Murray, the South African pastor, studied the prayers in Paul’s letters to learn how to pray for others. He saw that this first prayer in Ephesians is a prayer for light:

“In the former (i. 15), he prays for the Spirit of wisdom to enlighten them to know what their calling was, what their inheritance, what the mighty power of God working in them. Spiritual enlightenment and knowledge was their great need, to be obtained for them by prayer.”

Andrew Murray, The Ministry of Intercession

Notice Murray’s last words: “to be obtained for them by prayer.” Paul did not think that teaching alone would open their eyes. He had taught them for three years. Now he prayed, because only God can give sight.

John Calvin, the French Reformer who taught in Geneva in the 1500s, made the same point from this verse:

“You now hear that all wisdom and revelation is the gift of God.”

John Calvin, Institutes of the Christian Religion

Jesus Himself said, “And eternal life is this: that they know You, the only true God, and the one You sent, Jesus Christ” (John 17:3). Knowing God is not an extra for very spiritual people. It is what we were made for. That is why Paul, with every kind of need in front of him, put this request first.

Three key insights

  1. The greatest thing we can ask for anyone is that they would know God better. Health, safety and daily bread matter, and God cares about them. But Paul shows that the deepest prayer for a friend is that the Spirit would open the eyes of their heart to God Himself.
  2. Paul’s prayers begin with thanks for what God has already done. Before he asked for anything, he thanked God for the faith and love he saw in these believers. Thanks opens our own eyes to God’s work, and it makes our asking full of hope.
  3. The power that raised Jesus from the dead is at work for those who believe. We often feel weak, and we are. But Paul wants us to see that the strength behind our lives is the same strength that raised Christ and set Him above every power.

For us today

Many churches around the world have long prayer lists. That is a good thing. But if you listen to what is asked, most of the requests are about bodies, jobs, travel and exams. Those are real needs, and we should keep praying for them. Paul’s prayer invites us to add something: “Lord, let my brother know You better. Open my daughter’s eyes. Show my pastor Your power.”

This prayer is for every believer, not only the educated. In many places Christians have few books and little training. Some cannot read at all. Yet the Spirit who gives wisdom and revelation is given to them as fully as to any scholar. A grandmother in a mountain village may know God more deeply than a professor of theology, because her heart’s eyes have been opened.

And remember where this prayer was written. Paul was a prisoner. He could easily have prayed only for his own release. Instead, he used his time in chains to pray that others would see God. If you are shut in today, by illness, by old age, by caring for a sick relative, or even by prison, you can still pray this prayer. Some of the most powerful prayer in the church has come from people who could not go anywhere.

In the next chapter we will look at Paul’s second prayer in this letter. The first is a prayer for light. The second is a prayer for strength and love.

Try this

This week, pray Paul’s prayer for the people God has given you.

  • Start with thanks. Choose three people: a family member, a friend and a church leader. Thank God for one sign of His work that you see in each of them.
  • Pray the prayer by name. Read Ephesians 1:16-19 aloud. Where it says “you,” put the person’s name: “Father of glory, give Maria the Spirit who brings wisdom and revelation, so that she may come to know You.”
  • Pray it for yourself. Ask God to open the eyes of your own heart as you read the Bible this week. Before you read, pray, “LORD, open my eyes so that I can see.”
  • Write down what you see. At the end of each day, note one thing you learned about who God is.

A closing prayer

God of our Lord Jesus Christ, Father of glory, thank You for every person who trusts You and loves Your people. I ask You to give me, and those I love, the Spirit who brings wisdom and revelation, so that we may know You. Open the eyes of our hearts. Show us the hope of Your call. Teach us that we are Your inheritance, precious to You. And let us see Your great power, the power that raised Jesus from the dead, at work in our ordinary lives. In His name I pray. Amen.

Questions for reflection

  • When you pray for others, what do you usually ask for? What would change if you prayed Paul’s prayer for them?
  • Paul speaks of “how rich and glorious an inheritance He has in His holy people.” What does it mean to you that you are part of God’s inheritance?
  • Where in your life do you most need to see God’s power at work?

  • E. M. Bounds, Prayer and Praying Men, especially “Paul, the Teacher of Prayer”
  • Andrew Murray, The Inner Chamber, especially “The Heart and the Understanding”

fields.title: Rooted Deep in Love
fields.body_html:
“I pray that, in keeping with the riches of His glory, He will give you power, making your inner self strong through His Spirit, so that through faith and in love Christ will make His home in your hearts. You are rooted deep and set on a firm foundation, and I pray that you will have the strength to grasp, with all God’s holy people, the breadth and length and height and depth, and to know the love of Christ, a love that goes beyond knowledge, so that you may be filled up to all the fullness of God.” (Ephesians 3:16-19)

Paul starts to pray, and then stops.

At the beginning of the third chapter of Ephesians he writes, “For this reason I, Paul, the prisoner of Christ Jesus for the sake of you Gentiles” (Ephesians 3:1). And then the sentence breaks off. It is as if a new thought rushed in and he had to say it first. Paul seems often to have spoken his letters aloud while a helper wrote them down (Romans 16:22), and here we can almost hear him pause.

The thought that rushed in was the wonder of the gospel. For centuries a wall had stood between Jews and the other nations, the Gentiles. In the great temple in Jerusalem, a stone barrier kept non-Jews out of the inner courts. Now, Paul says, Christ “has broken down the wall that divided them” (Ephesians 2:14). “This is the mystery: through the gospel the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and sharers together in the promise in Christ Jesus” (Ephesians 3:6). Paul, once the strictest of Jews, had been sent to tell the nations this good news. He calls himself “less than the least of all God’s holy people” (Ephesians 3:8), and yet he was chosen for this.

He also knew that his readers were troubled. Their teacher was in prison. So he wrote, “I ask you not to lose heart over the troubles I bear for your sake” (Ephesians 3:13).

Then he comes back to his prayer, and this time he finishes it. “For this reason I kneel before the Father, from whom every family in heaven and on earth takes its name” (Ephesians 3:14-15).

In Paul’s day, Jews commonly stood to pray. Jesus Himself spoke of the time “whenever you stand up to pray” (Mark 11:25). Kneeling was for moments of special need or deep feeling. Solomon knelt at the dedication of the temple. Daniel knelt three times a day in a foreign land. Jesus knelt in Gethsemane. We do not know whether Paul’s chains let him kneel on the floor as he spoke these words, or whether he meant it as a picture of his heart. Either way, he is telling us: this prayer comes from the deepest place in me.

And notice to whom he kneels: the Father of every family. Jew and Gentile, slave and free, the believers in Ephesus and the prisoner in chains. One Father, one family. It is for this family that Paul now prays one of the greatest prayers in the Bible.

What Paul asked for

In the last chapter we looked at Paul’s first prayer in this letter, a prayer for light: that the believers would see who God is and what He has given them. This second prayer is a prayer for strength and for love. The first asks God to open their eyes. The second asks Him to fill their hearts.

Strength on the inside. Paul asks that God would give them power, “making your inner self strong through His Spirit.” He does not ask that their troubles would end. He asks that they would be strong inside while the troubles go on. He wrote to another church, “Our outer self may be decaying, but our inner self is being made new day after day” (2 Corinthians 4:16).

Christ at home. Next, he prays that Christ would “make His home” in their hearts. They already belonged to Christ. But a guest who stays for one night is different from a family member who lives in every room. Paul wants Christ to be at home in all of their lives, welcome everywhere.

Roots and a foundation. Paul uses two pictures. A tree has deep roots, so that it stands in the storm and stays green in the dry season (Jeremiah 17:8). A house has a firm foundation, so that “it did not fall, because its foundation was on rock” (Matthew 7:25). And the soil, the rock, under both is love.

A love too big to measure. Then Paul runs out of ordinary words. He prays that they would grasp “the breadth and length and height and depth” of the love of Christ, and that they would know “a love that goes beyond knowledge.” We can know it truly, but we will never reach the end of it. And he says we grasp it “with all God’s holy people.” No one learns the size of Christ’s love alone. The old saint and the new believer, the African and the Asian and the European, each see part of it, and together we see more.

The prayer ends in praise

Paul’s prayer is so large that he seems to worry his readers will think he has asked too much. So he ends with a song of praise:

“Now to the one who is able to do all things, far beyond anything we ask or think, by the power that is at work in us, to Him be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus, to every generation, for ever and ever. Amen.” (Ephesians 3:20-21)

Many churches still speak these words at the close of worship. They tell us that our biggest prayers are still small compared to what God is able to do.

Andrew Murray, looking at the things Paul asked for here, wrote:

“These were things that could only come direct from heaven; these were things he asked and expected. If we want to learn Paul’s art of intercession, we must ask nothing less for believers in our days.”

Andrew Murray, The Ministry of Intercession

And Charles Spurgeon, the London preacher, often reminded his people that our asking is too small:

“We could ask, if we were but more sensible and had more faith, for the very greatest things, but God is willing to give us infinitely more than we ask for!”

Charles H. Spurgeon, Mighty Power in Prayer

Three key insights

  1. Paul asks first for strength on the inside, not for an easier life on the outside. He was in chains and his friends were discouraged, yet he prayed for inner strength through the Spirit. God often answers our troubles by making us strong within them.
  2. We learn the love of Christ together with all God’s holy people. The love of Christ is too wide, long, high and deep for one person to grasp alone. Each believer, in every nation, helps the others to see more of it.
  3. God is able to do far beyond anything we ask or think. Paul’s great prayer ends in praise, because God is greater than our greatest requests. We can pray big prayers, knowing that we will never ask too much of Him.

For us today

Many Christians around the world live in hard places. Some face danger for their faith. Some face hunger, sickness or war. Some live with a quiet loneliness that no one sees. Paul’s prayer does not promise that these things will vanish. It promises something deeper: a strength inside that the troubles cannot break, and a love that holds us when everything else is shaking.

This prayer is also a cure for a small faith. In some churches the people are poor, and they have learned to ask God only for enough to get through the day. In other churches the people are comfortable, and they hardly ask God for anything. Paul’s prayer lifts both. It teaches the poor that they may ask for the “fullness of God.” It teaches the comfortable that they still need roots.

And it reminds us that we belong to one family. When you pray this prayer, pray it for believers you will never meet: the church in a country at war, the house church that meets in secret, the small congregation in a city far from yours. They are your brothers and sisters, named by the same Father. We will understand the love of Christ better when we pray for them and learn from them.

Try this

This week, let Paul’s second prayer shape your own.

  • Kneel, if you are able. Once each day, kneel to pray, as Paul did. If your body does not allow it, bow your head or open your hands. Let your posture say, “Father, this matters to me.”
  • Pray Ephesians 3:16-19 for someone in trouble. Choose one person who is going through a hard time. Pray each part for them: inner strength, Christ at home in their heart, roots in love, and the knowledge of Christ’s love.
  • Pray for the family. Choose one country where Christians suffer, and pray this prayer for the believers there.
  • End with praise. Close each time of prayer by saying Ephesians 3:20-21 aloud.

A closing prayer

Father, I kneel before You. Every family in heaven and on earth takes its name from You, and I thank You that I belong to Your family. Out of the riches of Your glory, make my inner self strong through Your Spirit. Let Christ make His home in my heart, in every room. Root me deep in His love and set me on its firm foundation. Help me, with all Your holy people, to grasp how wide and long and high and deep that love is, and fill me with all Your fullness. You are able to do far more than I ask or think. To You be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus, for ever and ever. Amen.

Questions for reflection

  • Paul prayed for inner strength rather than for his troubles to end. Which do you usually pray for, and why?
  • Are there “rooms” in your life where Christ is not yet at home?
  • How has another believer, perhaps from a different culture or background, helped you to see more of Christ’s love?

  • E. M. Bounds, The Reality of Prayer, especially “The Holy Spirit and Prayer”
  • Charles H. Spurgeon, Mighty Power in Prayer, especially “Ask and Have”

fields.title: When We Do Not Know What to Pray
fields.body_html:
“In the same way, the Spirit also lends a hand in our weakness. What we should pray for, and how, we do not know. But the Spirit Himself pleads on our behalf, with groans that no words carry.” (Romans 8:26)

It is probably about the year AD 57, and Paul is most likely in Corinth, a busy port city in southern Greece. He is staying in the home of a believer named Gaius, “who is host to me and to the whole church” (Romans 16:23). Soon he will sail for Jerusalem, carrying a gift of money from the Greek churches for the poor believers there (Romans 15:25-26). After that he hopes, at last, to visit Rome.

He has never been to Rome. He has never met most of the Christians there. So before he comes, he sends a letter, the longest of all his letters that we have. A man named Tertius sits with a pen and writes down the words as Paul speaks them (Romans 16:22).

By the time they reach the eighth chapter, Paul has explained the heart of the gospel. All people have sinned. Christ died for us and rose again. Those who trust Him are declared righteous, set free and given the Holy Spirit. “In the Spirit we call out, ‘Abba, Father!’” (Romans 8:15). We are God’s children.

But Paul is honest. God’s children still suffer. Paul himself had been beaten, stoned, shipwrecked and thrown in prison. Within a few years the believers in Rome would face worse. So he turns to the question every suffering Christian asks: if we are God’s children, why does life still hurt so much?

His answer begins with a wide view. He looks at the whole world:

“We know that all creation, to this very day, groans as one and suffers the pains of giving birth together. And not creation alone. We ourselves, who have the Spirit as the first share of the harvest, also groan within ourselves while we long for our adoption as children, when our body will be redeemed.” (Romans 8:22-23)

Creation groans. The fields dry up, sickness spreads, animals and people die. We groan too. Our bodies grow weak, our hearts break, and we long for the day when everything will be made new. But Paul calls it the groaning of a woman giving birth. It is real pain, but it is pain that leads to new life.

And then Paul says something astonishing. There is a third groan. “In the same way,” he says, the Spirit groans too. When we are too weak to pray, when we do not even know what to ask for, the Holy Spirit of God prays for us, “with groans that no words carry.”

In Volume 2 we heard this verse twice in passing. Now we stop and listen to it in full.

What Paul teaches

First, Paul admits our weakness in prayer. “What we should pray for, and how, we do not know.” This is the great apostle speaking. He had seen the risen Christ. He had planted churches from Syria to Greece. And still he says, “we do not know.” There is no shame in being confused in prayer. It is part of being human in a broken world.

Second, the Spirit “lends a hand.” The picture is of someone who comes alongside to carry a heavy load with us. He does not take the weight away and leave. He shares it.

Third, the Spirit “pleads on our behalf.” He is not a distant helper. He lives within us, and from within He brings our needs to the Father.

Fourth, God understands the Spirit’s prayer, even when we do not:

“And God, who looks deep into hearts, knows what the Spirit intends, because the Spirit pleads for God’s holy people in line with what God wants.” (Romans 8:27)

Here is great comfort. Our prayers may be confused, but the Spirit’s prayer is not. He always prays “in line with what God wants.” So when we cannot find the right words, the right prayer is still being prayed.

Christians have understood the “groans” in different ways. Some think they are the Spirit’s own groans, deeper than any human language. Others think the Spirit takes up our sighs and tears and turns them into prayer. Some link them with the gift of tongues, while many others do not. We do not need to settle the question to receive the comfort. Either way, no sigh of a believer is wasted. The psalmist said, “Lord, You see everything I long for; not one of my sighs escapes You” (Psalm 38:9).

And notice what comes next. Right after the Spirit’s prayer, Paul writes, “We know that, for people who love God, all things work together and lead to good” (Romans 8:28). That famous verse is not a cheerful slogan. It stands right beside our groaning and the Spirit’s prayer. God is at work for good, and part of how He works is by the Spirit praying in us.

How the Spirit helps us pray

Andrew Murray, the South African pastor, wrote to Christians who felt their prayers were too poor to matter:

“When you cannot find words, when your words appear cold and feeble, just believe: The Holy Spirit is praying in me.”

Andrew Murray, The Ministry of Intercession

R. A. Torrey, the American Bible teacher, saw in Romans 8:27 a way the Spirit guides our requests:

“Here we are distinctly told that the Spirit of God prays in us, draws out our prayer, in the line of God’s will.”

R. A. Torrey, How to Pray

And E. M. Bounds noticed that the Spirit’s groaning is not only for our private troubles. It reaches out to the whole groaning world:

“He inspires us to this most Divine work of intercession, and His strength enables us to sigh unto God for the oppressed, the burdened and the distressed creation.”

E. M. Bounds, The Reality of Prayer

So the Spirit helps us in two ways. Sometimes He prays for us when we have no words at all. And sometimes He gives us words, a burden, a name or a need that we cannot stop praying about. A few verses later Paul adds that Christ Jesus is “at the right hand of God, where He pleads on our behalf” (Romans 8:34). The Son prays for us in heaven. The Spirit prays in us on earth. We are never praying alone.

Three key insights

  1. Not knowing what to pray is not a failure; it is where the Spirit’s help begins. Paul himself said “we do not know.” When our words run out, we have not come to the end of prayer, only to the end of ourselves.
  2. The Holy Spirit prays for us, and the Son prays for us too. The Spirit pleads within us and Christ pleads at the Father’s right hand. Our weak prayers are carried by two Divine helpers.
  3. The Spirit always prays in line with what God wants. Even when we ask for the wrong things, the Spirit’s prayer is right. We can trust our requests, and ourselves, to God’s good will.

For us today

There are times when everyone runs out of words. A mother sits beside a child with a high fever, far from any hospital. A family waits for news after a flood or an earthquake. A believer is in a prison cell, or a refugee camp, or a hospital bed, too tired to think. A widow kneels by her bed, and all she can say is the name of Jesus. Paul’s words are for these moments. The Spirit is praying. God is listening. Nothing is lost.

This truth also frees us from fear of praying “wrongly.” Some believers hardly pray because they think they do not know the right words. Some think only pastors or educated people can pray properly. Romans 8 tells us that every believer has the same Helper. A child’s broken words, a farmer’s tired sigh and a scholar’s careful prayer all reach the Father through the same Spirit.

And Romans 8 widens our prayer. The Spirit groans with a groaning creation. When we see war, hunger, injustice or the damage done to God’s world, we may feel too small to pray. But the Spirit can give us a share in His longing for the day when God makes all things new. Our sighs for a broken world can become prayer.

Try this

This week, practice relying on the Spirit when you pray.

  • Begin with honesty. Start your prayer time by saying, “Father, I do not know how to pray as I should. Holy Spirit, help me.”
  • Be still and bring your sighs. Think of the burden that weighs on you most. If you cannot find words, sit quietly before God with it. Trust that the Spirit is praying.
  • Listen for a burden. Ask the Spirit to put one person or one need on your heart. Pray for it each day, and notice if the burden grows.
  • Pray for the groaning world. Choose one place in the news where people are suffering. Read Romans 8:22-23 and bring that place to God.

A closing prayer

Father, I do not always know what to pray for, or how. Sometimes my words are cold and weak, and sometimes I have no words at all. Thank You that Your Holy Spirit lives in me and lends a hand in my weakness. Thank You that He pleads for me with groans that no words carry, and always in line with what You want. Thank You that Jesus, at Your right hand, pleads for me too. Teach me to rest in Your help, to bring You my sighs, and to long with all creation for the day when You make everything new. Amen.

Questions for reflection

  • Have you ever felt that you did not know what to pray? What did you do?
  • How does it help to know that the Spirit always prays “in line with what God wants”?
  • What is one burden for the wider world that you could carry to God this week?

fields.title: Always Wrestling in Prayer
fields.body_html:
“Epaphras, one of your own and a servant of Christ, sends you greetings. He always wrestles for you in his prayers, asking that you will stand firm, mature and fully sure of everything God wills.” (Colossians 4:12)

Near the end of the letter to the Colossians, Paul names the friends around him. It is a short list. Tychicus, who will bring the Colossians his news. Onesimus, a slave who has become a brother in Christ. Aristarchus, Mark, Luke the doctor, Demas. Most readers move through such lists quickly.

But in the middle of them Paul stops to say a little more about one man. His name is Epaphras.

Epaphras came from Colossae, a small town in the valley of the Lycus River, in the Roman province of Asia, in what is now western Turkey. Two larger cities stood a few hours’ walk away: Laodicea and Hierapolis. Paul had never visited Colossae. He tells them that he is struggling for them and “for everyone who has never met me in person” (Colossians 2:1). So how did the gospel get there?

Through Epaphras. Paul tells the Colossians that they first heard the gospel and “came to know God’s grace in all its truth” from him: “You learned it from Epaphras, our dear fellow servant, who serves Christ faithfully on our behalf” (Colossians 1:6-7). Many think that Epaphras heard the good news during Paul’s long stay in Ephesus, when “all the people of the province of Asia, Jews and Greeks alike, heard the word of the Lord” (Acts 19:10), and then carried it home to his own valley. That is a likely guess, but the Bible does not tell us.

Now Epaphras was far from home. He had traveled to Paul, who was in chains. In the short letter to Philemon, probably written at about the same time, Paul even calls him “my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus” (Philemon 1:23). We do not know whether Epaphras was arrested too, or whether he chose to share Paul’s confinement. Either way, he could not simply go home.

He may have come with worrying news. The letter to the Colossians warns against teaching that was leading believers away from Christ: “Watch out, so that no one carries you off like captives by means of philosophy that is empty deceit” (Colossians 2:8). Epaphras loved these people. He had brought them to Christ. Now they were in danger, and he was far away.

What could he do? He could not preach to them. He could not visit them. But he could pray. And Paul, who was with him, tells us how he prayed: “He always wrestles for you in his prayers.” Then Paul adds, “I can vouch for him that he works hard for you and for the believers in Laodicea and Hierapolis” (Colossians 4:13).

Paul had seen many people pray. This man’s praying was so remarkable that Paul wrote to Colossae about it.

Who he was

Epaphras is easy to miss. He wrote no book of the Bible. No miracle is linked to his name. Some readers confuse him with Epaphroditus, a messenger from the church in Philippi (Philippians 2:25). The names are related, but most think they were two different men from two different places.

Yet Epaphras was a church planter, a pastor and a man of prayer. Paul gives him three titles of honor: “our dear fellow servant,” “a servant of Christ,” and “one of your own.” He was not a famous outsider. He was a local man who loved his own people, and his whole heart was bound up with three small churches in one valley.

How he prayed

Notice four things about the prayer of Epaphras.

He prayed always. Paul does not say Epaphras prayed for them once, or when he remembered. He says “always.” Their names were part of his daily life.

He prayed hard. The word “wrestles” tells us that this prayer was a struggle. Paul uses a word from the same family when he speaks of his own work, “struggling by His energy, which is powerfully at work in me” (Colossians 1:29), and when he asks the Romans to “join me in my struggle through your prayers to God for me” (Romans 15:30). It is the family of words from which we get the English word “agony.” Luke uses a related word for Jesus in the garden: “In His anguish He prayed all the more intensely” (Luke 22:44). Real prayer for others can be hard work.

E. M. Bounds explained what the word means:

“The word means to enter into a contest, to fight against adversaries. It means, moreover, to engage with fervent zeal to endeavour to obtain.”

E. M. Bounds, The Necessity of Prayer

We do not wrestle against God, as if He were unwilling. We wrestle against everything that would pull our loved ones away from Him, and against our own laziness and distraction.

He prayed for others. Epaphras was a prisoner, or near to one. He had his own needs. But Paul says he wrestled “for you.”

He prayed for what matters most. He did not only ask that the Colossians would be safe or comfortable. He asked “that you will stand firm, mature and fully sure of everything God wills.” He wanted them to stand firm against false teaching, to grow up in Christ, and to be sure of God’s will for their lives. It is the same goal Paul had in all his work: “so that we may bring every person before God mature in Christ” (Colossians 1:28).

Bounds saw that this hidden prayer was as important as any sermon:

“Epaphras did as much or more by prayer for the Colossian saints than by his preaching.”

E. M. Bounds, Power Through Prayer

Three key insights

  1. When we cannot be with the people we love, we can still fight for them in prayer. Epaphras was far away and unable to help in person. Prayer was the one way he could still work for his people, and Paul says it was real work.
  2. Prayer for others is often hard, and that is no sign that it is wrong. Paul says Epaphras “wrestles.” Sometimes prayer feels like a struggle. That struggle is not failure; it is love refusing to give up.
  3. The best prayer for others asks that they will stand firm and grow mature in God’s will. Epaphras prayed for more than comfort. He asked that his friends would be strong, grown up in Christ and sure of everything God wants.

For us today

Many believers today live far from the people they love most. A father works in another country to send money home. A mother cleans houses in a distant city. Students leave their villages to study. Refugees are scattered across borders. Missionaries and pastors are sent away from their own churches. All of them know the pain of Epaphras: “I cannot be there.” His story says: you can still be there in prayer.

Epaphras also speaks to those who serve in hidden places. In many churches around the world there are faithful people whose names no one outside their town will ever know: a pastor of a small congregation, a grandmother who prays every morning for every child on her street, an elder who has prayed for the same village for forty years. Heaven knows their names, as Paul knew the name of Epaphras. In Volume 4 we will meet the desert mothers and fathers, who saw prayer as a struggle to the last breath.

And Epaphras teaches us to pray for our own church. It is easy to complain about a church’s weaknesses. Epaphras did something better. He wrestled in prayer for it. If your church is struggling with division, false teaching, discouragement or persecution, your prayers may be the most important thing you can give.

Try this

This week, take up the work of Epaphras for the people God has given you.

  • Make a short list. Write down the names of the people you are responsible for or closest to: your family, your small group, your church, perhaps your town. Keep the list where you pray.
  • Pray for one name each day with focus. Instead of praying quickly for everyone, take time with one person. Ask that they will “stand firm, mature and fully sure of everything God wills.”
  • Pray for someone far away. Choose one person you love who lives at a distance. Pray for them by name each day, and let them know that you are praying.
  • Keep going when it is hard. If your mind wanders or you feel nothing, keep praying. That is part of the wrestling.

A closing prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for Epaphras, a servant who loved his people and wrestled for them in prayer. Forgive me for the times I have prayed for others carelessly, or not at all. Give me his love and his faithfulness. Teach me to pray always for the people You have given me, near and far. Help me to keep praying when it is hard. And answer my prayers by making those I love stand firm, mature and fully sure of everything God wills. For Your name’s sake. Amen.

Questions for reflection

  • Who has prayed for you faithfully, perhaps without your knowing? How has it shaped your life?
  • What makes praying for others feel like hard work for you?
  • Which people or which church has God placed on your heart to “wrestle” for in prayer?
