  • E. M. Bounds, The Necessity of Prayer, especially “Prayer and Fervency”
  • Andrew Murray, The Ministry of Intercession, especially “God Seeks Intercessors”

fields.title: Do Not Worry About Anything
fields.body_html:
“Do not worry about anything. Instead, in everything, bring your requests to God through prayer and petition, with thanksgiving. And God’s peace, which is beyond all our understanding, will stand guard over your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.” (Philippians 4:6-7)

The apostle Paul was a prisoner. Most think he wrote his letter to the Philippians from Rome, in the early 60s AD, though some think it came from an earlier imprisonment in Ephesus. Luke ends the book of Acts with Paul in Rome, waiting for his trial before the emperor:

“Once we were in Rome, Paul was given permission to live in private quarters, though a soldier guarded him.” (Acts 28:16)

So picture a small rented room in Rome, the capital of the empire. A Roman soldier sits by the door. Paul wears a chain (Acts 28:20). The soldiers take turns, so over the months a great many of them come to know why this man is there (Philippians 1:13). Visitors come and go. Paul cannot.

He had every reason to worry. His trial was coming, and it might end in his death. He wrote openly that Christ would be honored in his body “whether through my life or through my death” (Philippians 1:20). Some preachers in the city were using his time in prison to make themselves look important (Philippians 1:15-17). Far away in Philippi, two women who had worked beside him, Euodia and Syntyche, could not agree, and Paul had to plead with them to be of one mind in the Lord (Philippians 4:2). And his friend Epaphroditus, who had traveled all the way from Philippi to bring him a gift, had fallen ill. Paul wrote, “He really was sick, so sick he almost died” (Philippians 2:27).

The Philippians knew what Paul’s prisons were like. Years before, in their own city, he and Silas had been beaten and locked in the stocks, and at midnight they had prayed and “sang praises to God” (Acts 16:25). Now he was in chains again. What would he write to them?

He wrote a letter full of joy. And near the end, with the soldier still sitting by the door, he wrote the words of our key verse: “Do not worry about anything.” Then he chose a soldier’s word for what God’s peace would do. It would “stand guard” over their hearts and minds.

Paul knew what a guard looked like. He saw one every day.

A man with reasons to worry

It would be easy to read this verse as the advice of a man with an easy life. It is the opposite. Paul did not pretend that nothing troubled him. In another letter he wrote about “my anxious care for all the churches” (2 Corinthians 11:28). He loved people, and love always carries a weight.

So when Paul says, “Do not worry about anything,” he does not mean, “Stop caring.” In the same letter he praises Timothy because he will “truly care about your welfare” (Philippians 2:20). Caring is good. Worry is caring that has nowhere to go. It turns around and around inside us, like water in a closed pot over a fire.

Paul gives the care somewhere to go. “Instead,” he says. Instead of worrying, pray. The verse does not take the burden away. It changes where we carry it.

Just before this he wrote a short sentence that holds the whole secret: “The Lord is near” (Philippians 4:5). He is near in two ways. He is near in place: He is with us now, in the room, beside the bed, at the prison door. And He is near in time: Jesus is coming soon. A believer who knows that the Lord is near can bring Him anything.

How Paul taught us to pray about worry

Look closely at the verse. It gives us four things.

First, everything. “In everything” means that no worry is too small or too large. The school fees, the sick child, the angry neighbor, the letter from the government, the fear that keeps us awake at three in the morning: all of it may be brought to God.

Second, requests. Paul uses three words: “prayer and petition” and “requests.” He wants us to be specific. Worry is often vague, a cloud of fear with no edges. Prayer gives it edges. We name the thing and hand it over.

Third, thanksgiving. Even while we ask, we thank God for what He has already done and for who He is. Thanksgiving reminds a worried heart that God has been faithful before.

Charles Spurgeon, the London preacher, once preached a whole sermon on this verse. He called it “Prayer, the Cure for Care,” and he said:

“Cares are numerous and, therefore, let your prayers be as numerous. Turn everything that is a care into a prayer.”

Charles H. Spurgeon, Mighty Power in Prayer

He went on to say that our cares should be “the raw material of your prayers.” Raw material is what a builder or a weaver starts with: wood, stone, cotton. Spurgeon means that our worries are not wasted. Each one can become a prayer.

The American teacher R. A. Torrey made the same point in simple words:

“Just keep in constant touch with God, and when any trouble or vexation, great or small, comes up, speak to Him about it, never forgetting to return thanks for what He has already done.”

R. A. Torrey, How to Pray

Fourth, and last, comes the result. Notice what Paul promises and what he does not promise. He does not say, “Pray, and everything will turn out as you want.” Paul himself did not know how his trial would end. He promises something deeper: “God’s peace, which is beyond all our understanding, will stand guard over your hearts and your minds.”

This peace is “beyond all our understanding.” Other people may not understand it. We may not understand it ourselves. The trouble is still there, but so is the guard. Paul goes on a few verses later to say that he had learned to be content in hunger and in plenty, and that “I have strength for every situation in the One who makes me strong” (Philippians 4:13). He had learned it. Peace is a gift, but it is also a lesson, practiced one worry at a time.

Three key insights

  1. Worry is a signal to pray, not a secret to hide. Paul did not tell the Philippians to pretend they were not afraid. He told them to turn each fear into a request. Every worry can become a doorway into the presence of God.
  2. Thanksgiving belongs inside every request. When we thank God while we ask, we remember His past kindness. A thankful heart finds it harder to believe that God has forgotten us.
  3. God’s peace can guard us before our circumstances change. Paul was still in chains when he wrote these words. The promise is not that every problem will disappear, but that God’s peace will stand guard over our hearts and minds, whatever comes.

For us today

Some of the Christians reading these words are in prison for their faith, as Paul was. Some are waiting for news from a doctor, or from a son who has gone to work in another country, or from an office that decides whether their family may stay. Some do not know where next month’s rent will come from. Some farmers are watching the sky for rain. Worry is a language spoken in every land.

To each of us, Paul says the same thing: bring it to God. Bring it in detail. Bring it with thanks. And let Him guard your heart.

One word of care. Some people live with an anxiety that does not go away, an illness of the mind that makes the heart race and sleep flee. If that is you, this verse is not a scolding. You are not failing God because you feel afraid. Keep bringing your fears to Him, and do not be ashamed to seek help from a wise friend, a pastor, or a doctor. God can give His peace through prayer, through people and through medicine. The God who cared for Epaphroditus in his sickness cares for you in yours.

Paul also shows us what to do with our minds once we have prayed. In the next verse he says, “let your minds dwell on these things”: all that is true, honorable, just, pure and lovely (Philippians 4:8). After we hand our worries to God, we do not need to keep picking them up again. We can fill our minds with good things.

Try this

This week, practice turning worry into prayer.

  • Write a worry list. Each evening, write down the things that are worrying you, one line each. Be specific.
  • Turn each line into a request. Beside each worry, write a short prayer: “Father, please...” Then say it aloud to God.
  • Add one thanksgiving. For every request, thank God for one thing He has already done, in that part of your life or in another.
  • Let the guard stand. When the same worry comes back, do not argue with it for an hour. Say quietly, “I have given this to You, Lord. The Lord is near,” and turn your mind to something true and good.

A closing prayer

Lord Jesus, You are near. You were near to Paul in his chains, and You are near to me now. I bring You the things that worry me: the large ones and the small ones, the ones I can name and the ones I cannot. I turn each one into a request, and I thank You for all You have already done. I do not ask You to explain everything to me. I ask for Your peace, the peace that is beyond my understanding. Let it stand guard over my heart and my mind today, tonight, and every day until I see You. Amen.

Questions for reflection

  • What are you most worried about today? What would it look like to turn that worry into a specific request?
  • Why do you think Paul joins thanksgiving to prayer about worry?
  • Paul says he had “learned” to be content. What has God taught you through times of worry in the past?

  • R. A. Torrey, How to Pray, especially “Praying with Thanksgiving”
  • Charles H. Spurgeon, The Cheque Book of the Bank of Faith, especially “The Month of March”

fields.title: Never Stop Praying
fields.body_html:
“Be joyful at all times. Never stop praying. Whatever happens, give thanks; this is what God wants for you in Christ Jesus.” (1 Thessalonians 5:16-18)

Thessalonica was a busy port city in Macedonia, in the north of Greece. A great Roman road ran through it, and ships came and went from its harbor. When Paul and Silas arrived there, not long after their night in the prison at Philippi, they went to the synagogue.

“As he usually did, Paul went to the synagogue, and on three Sabbaths he reasoned with them from the Scriptures, opening them up and laying out the case that the Christ had to suffer and rise from the dead.” (Acts 17:2-3)

Some Jews believed, and so did a large number of Greeks who worshiped God, and quite a few leading women of the city. A new church was born. But very soon there was trouble. A mob gathered and attacked the house of a believer named Jason, looking for Paul and Silas. When they could not find them, they dragged Jason and some other believers before the city officials, shouting that these Christians “defy Caesar’s decrees and say there is another king, one called Jesus” (Acts 17:7). That same night the believers sent Paul and Silas away in secret.

So the young church was left alone. They were new to the faith. Most had only just “turned to God from idols” (1 Thessalonians 1:9). They had no New Testament, no church building, and no pastor with years of training. And they were suffering for their faith from their own people (1 Thessalonians 2:14).

Paul could not stop thinking about them. He traveled on to Athens, but his heart was still in Thessalonica. At last he could bear it no longer, and he sent Timothy back to see how they were.

“So, when we could not bear the waiting any longer, we decided to stay behind in Athens on our own and sent you Timothy, our brother and God’s fellow worker in the gospel of Christ.” (1 Thessalonians 3:1-2)

Then Timothy came back with wonderful news. The believers were standing firm. Their faith and love were growing. Paul was so glad that he sat down and wrote them a letter. Many think it is the earliest letter of Paul that we have, written from Corinth around AD 50.

Near the end of that letter, Paul gives the new believers three short commands, one after the other. Be joyful. Never stop praying. Give thanks.

Who they were

It helps to know who first heard the words “never stop praying.” They were not monks or full-time ministers. They were ordinary working people in a busy city. Paul told them to “earn your living with your hands” (1 Thessalonians 4:11). Perhaps some worked in the market or at the docks. Some may have been slaves in other people’s houses.

Paul himself worked with his hands while he was among them. He was a tentmaker by trade (Acts 18:3), and he reminded them:

“You remember, brothers and sisters, how hard we worked and toiled: we labored night and day so as not to be a burden to any of you while we preached the gospel of God to you.” (1 Thessalonians 2:9)

Now listen to what he says about his prayers in the same letter: “Night and day we pray with great urgency to see you face to face” (1 Thessalonians 3:10). Night and day he worked. Night and day he prayed. The two went together. Paul was not praying instead of working. It seems that he prayed while he worked, with his tools in his hands.

So when he told the Thessalonians to “never stop praying,” he was not asking them to leave their work and kneel all day. He was asking them to do what he did.

What it means to never stop

How can anyone pray without stopping? We have to eat, sleep, work and talk to other people.

Paul uses the same kind of words about his own prayers in this letter. “Before our God and Father we never stop remembering” you, he says (1 Thessalonians 1:3). “We too give thanks to God without ceasing” (1 Thessalonians 2:13). He did not mean that he said nothing else all day. He meant that his prayer for them never ended. He kept coming back to it, again and again. It was like a fire that is never allowed to go out.

Charles Spurgeon preached a sermon on this one verse, and he noticed what comes just before it:

“It comes immediately after the precept, ‘Rejoice evermore;’ as if that command had somewhat staggered the reader, and made him ask ‘How can I always rejoice?’ and, therefore, the apostle appended as answer, ‘Always pray.’ The more praying the more rejoicing.”

Charles H. Spurgeon, Mighty Power in Prayer

In the same sermon Spurgeon said that “never stop praying” is not only a command. It is also an open door. A king might see visitors only on certain days. God sees His children at any hour:

“The dead of night is not too late for God; the breaking of the morning, when the first grey light is seen, is not too early for the Most High; at midday he is not too busy; and when the evening gathers he is not weary with his children’s prayers.”

Charles H. Spurgeon, Mighty Power in Prayer

So “never stop praying” means at least three things. It means keeping set times of prayer and not giving them up. It means turning to God many times during the day, in short prayers, as Nehemiah did when the king asked him a question: “So I prayed to the God of heaven, and I said to the king...” (Nehemiah 2:4-5). And it means living all day with a heart turned toward God, the way a mother who is busy with many tasks still keeps one ear open for her sleeping baby.

In later volumes we will meet Christians who gave their lives to this verse: a cook in a French monastery kitchen, a village of believers in Germany whose prayer, the story is told, went on day and night for about a hundred years, and a pilgrim in Russia who walked from place to place asking how to pray without ceasing.

Three key insights

  1. Praying without stopping is for ordinary working people. Paul wrote these words to working people, perhaps traders, dockworkers and servants, and he lived them himself while he made tents. Prayer does not need an empty day. It can run alongside our work like a song.
  2. Joy, prayer and thanks belong together. Paul did not give three separate rules. Prayer feeds joy, and joy leads to more prayer, and thanks rises out of both, “whatever happens.”
  3. God is never too busy for His children. Because heaven’s door is always open, there is no wrong hour to pray. We can turn to God at midnight, at dawn, and in the middle of the busiest day.

For us today

The Thessalonians were new believers in a hostile city. Many readers of this book know what that is like. Some are the only Christians in their family. Some live where their neighbors mock them or worse. Some cannot meet freely with other believers. Paul’s answer for them is not a long program. It is a life of joy, prayer and thanks, lived in the middle of the trouble.

“Whatever happens, give thanks.” Notice that Paul does not say, “Give thanks for whatever happens.” The persecution in Thessalonica was not good. Some of their loved ones had died, and they were grieving (1 Thessalonians 4:13). But in every situation there is still a reason to thank God: He is still our Father, Jesus is still coming, and nothing can take us out of His hand.

You may say, “But my life is too busy and too noisy to pray all day.” Think of the woman who carries water from the well, the man who drives a taxi through crowded streets, the student on a long bus ride, the nurse on the night shift. Each of these has many small moments: waiting, walking, washing, lifting. Each one can become a moment of prayer. You do not have to close your eyes or say the words aloud. You can simply say in your heart, “Lord, I am here. You are here. Help me.”

Try this

For one week, try to “never stop praying” in a few simple ways.

  • Keep one set time. Choose a time each day, even ten minutes, for unhurried prayer. Protect it.
  • Tie prayer to your tasks. Choose two things you do every day, such as washing your hands or starting a journey. Each time you do them, say a short prayer.
  • Pray for one person all day. Each morning, choose one person. Every time they come into your mind during the day, lift them to God in a single sentence.
  • End with thanks. Before you sleep, name three things you can thank God for today, “whatever happens.”

A closing prayer

Father, You are never too busy for me, and You never grow tired of my prayers. Teach me to pray without stopping. Help me to keep my times with You, and to turn to You again and again through the day, at my work, on the road and in my home. Fill me with joy that comes from You, and give me a thankful heart in every situation. As Paul prayed for the believers in Thessalonica night and day, help me to pray for others. And keep my heart turned toward You until Jesus comes. Amen.

Questions for reflection

  • Paul worked night and day, and prayed night and day. What would it look like for you to pray while you work?
  • How have you found that prayer and joy feed each other?
  • What is the difference between giving thanks in everything and giving thanks for everything?

  • R. A. Torrey, How to Pray, especially “When to Pray”

fields.title: For Kings and All in Authority
fields.body_html:
“First of all, then, I urge that requests, prayers, intercessions and thanks be offered for everyone: for kings and for all who hold high office, so that we may live peaceful and quiet lives, fully devoted to God and worthy of respect.” (1 Timothy 2:1-2)

Ephesus was one of the great cities of the Roman world. It stood on the west coast of what is now Turkey, with a harbor full of ships and streets full of traders. It was famous for its temple to the goddess Artemis, one of the wonders of the ancient world, and many people in the city made their living from her.

Paul had lived and preached in Ephesus for about three years. Many people turned from their idols to Christ, and the trade in idols began to suffer. A silversmith named Demetrius, who made little silver shrines of Artemis, gathered the other craftsmen and stirred them up. Soon the whole city was in an uproar. Luke tells us how the craftsmen answered Demetrius:

“On hearing this they flew into a rage, and they kept shouting, ‘Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!’” (Acts 19:28)

A huge crowd rushed into the open-air theater, and for about two hours they shouted the same words (Acts 19:34).

Later, Paul left his young helper Timothy in charge of the believers in Ephesus (1 Timothy 1:3). Timothy had grown up with a believing mother and grandmother (2 Timothy 1:5). He was still young, and some people looked down on him for it (1 Timothy 4:12). False teachers were troubling the church. Outside the church, the city still honored Artemis, and the empire still honored Caesar as a god.

Then a letter came from Paul. Many think it was written in the 60s AD, when the man on the throne in Rome was the emperor Nero.

Timothy must have wondered what Paul would say first. What should a small, threatened church do before anything else? Paul’s answer is our key verse. “First of all,” pray. Pray for everyone. And pray “for kings and for all who hold high office.”

Who they were praying for

It is surprising. The “kings” of Paul’s day were not Christian rulers. The emperor was a pagan who allowed himself to be worshiped. The governors and city officials were the men who could arrest Christians, beat them and throw them into prison. Paul knew this well. “Three times I was flogged with rods,” he wrote (2 Corinthians 11:25).

And if the letter comes from those years, the emperor was Nero. In AD 64, a great fire burned much of Rome, and Nero blamed the Christians. The Roman writer Tacitus tells us that many believers were put to death in terrible ways. An old tradition says that Paul himself was killed in Rome under Nero, and Peter too. These were the “kings” for whom the church was told to pray.

Yet Paul had also seen rulers do good. In Ephesus itself, it was the town clerk who calmed the rioting crowd and sent it home (Acts 19:35-41). Some high officials of the province were Paul’s friends and sent him a warning not to go into the theater (Acts 19:31). Paul knew that even pagan rulers could keep order, protect the weak and hold back violence. He had good reason to pray for them.

How the first Christians prayed for rulers

Look at what Paul asks for. He wants prayer for rulers “so that we may live peaceful and quiet lives.” The church is not asking for power. It is asking for peace, so that it can worship God, live honestly and share the good news.

Then Paul gives a deeper reason:

“This is good, and it pleases God our Savior, who wants everyone to be saved and to come to know the truth.” (1 Timothy 2:3-4)

“Everyone” includes kings. God wants rulers to be saved too. Paul knew this from his own story. He wrote in this same letter that he once used to “persecute His people and treat them violently. But I was shown mercy” (1 Timothy 1:13). If God could save Saul the persecutor, He could save a governor, a police chief or an emperor.

The first Christians took Paul’s words seriously. About a hundred and thirty years later, in Carthage in North Africa, Christians were still being arrested and killed. Tertullian, whom we met in chapter 3, wrote a defense of the faith to the Roman rulers. He told them plainly what Christians did when they met:

“Without ceasing, for all our emperors we offer prayer. We pray for life prolonged; for security to the empire; for protection to the imperial house; for brave armies, a faithful senate, a virtuous people, the world at rest, whatever, as man or Cæsar, an emperor would wish.”

Tertullian, The Apology

Think of that. The emperors were killing Christians, and the Christians were praying for the emperors’ long life. In Volume 4 we will hear a prayer for rulers from Clement of Rome, written by a church that knew the same danger.

Praying with wisdom

Praying for rulers who do evil raises honest questions. Does it mean we approve of what they do? Must we pray only for their success?

Scripture gives us a wise path. We pray for their good. We ask God to save them, to give them wisdom, and to make them just. The old prayer for Israel’s king asked God to help him “defend the poor among the people and bring rescue to needy families” (Psalm 72:4). That is a prayer we can pray for any ruler.

We pray without anger. Paul goes on: “So I want the men everywhere to pray, lifting up holy hands, free from anger and quarreling” (1 Timothy 2:8). It is possible to pray for a ruler with clenched teeth. Paul asks for something better.

We may also pray for justice. The Psalms ask God to “break the power of the wicked” (Psalm 10:15). Praying for a ruler does not mean pretending that cruelty is good. We can ask God both to bless a ruler and to stop the evil that ruler does.

And we stay faithful to God. Praying for rulers is not the same as obeying them in everything. When the leaders in Jerusalem ordered the apostles to stop preaching, Peter answered, “It is God we must obey rather than people” (Acts 5:29). The apostles respected authority, prayed for those in power, and still refused to deny Christ.

The American teacher R. A. Torrey saw a danger in his own day that is still with us:

“Christians can accomplish far more for “good government” by praying for than by railing at the powers that be.”

R. A. Torrey, What the Bible Teaches

“Railing” means complaining angrily. It is easy to complain about our leaders. It is harder, and better, to pray for them.

Three key insights

  1. Prayer for those in power comes first, not last. Paul put it at the head of his instructions for the church. Before programs and plans, the church is called to pray for the people who govern.
  2. God wants rulers to be saved, even the ones who persecute. The God who saved Saul the persecutor wants everyone to come to know the truth. No ruler is beyond the reach of His mercy, or of our prayers.
  3. We can pray for a ruler without approving of evil. We ask God to bless rulers with wisdom and salvation, to hold back their wrongs, and to bring justice. And we remain faithful to Christ, whatever they command.

For us today

Some readers of this book live under rulers who fear and oppose the church. Their pastors have been arrested. Their meetings are watched. For them, 1 Timothy 2 is not easy, but it is a path of freedom. Hatred can make us like the people we hate. Prayer keeps our hearts free.

Other readers live in countries where they can vote and speak freely. There, the danger is different. We may pray only for the leaders we like, and only complain about the others. Paul says “for everyone.” Pray for the leader you voted for and the one you did not. Pray for the president or king, but also for the mayor, the judge, the police officer in your street, the head of your village, the teacher in charge of your school.

The prophet Jeremiah once wrote to God’s people in exile in Babylon, a city that had destroyed their temple. He told them, “Seek the peace of the city where I have sent you as exiles, and pray to the LORD for it, since your own peace depends on its peace” (Jeremiah 29:7). Wherever we live, our prayers can be a blessing to our land.

Try this

This week, take Paul’s words “first of all” seriously.

  • Make a list. Write down the names of those who govern you, from the highest leader of your country to the leaders of your town or village.
  • Pray for one each day. Ask God to save them, give them wisdom, help them protect the poor, and hold back any evil they plan.
  • Watch your words. Each time you hear yourself complain about a leader, stop and pray one sentence for that person.
  • Remember the persecuted. Pray for believers who live under hostile rulers, and pray for those rulers by name if you can.

A closing prayer

Father, You rule over every king and every government. I pray for those who hold authority over me. Save them. Give them wisdom, honesty and courage. Help them protect the weak and the poor. Where they do wrong, hold them back and turn their hearts. Forgive me for the times I have complained about them instead of praying for them. Keep me faithful to You, whatever they decide. And give Your church peace, so that we may live quiet lives, fully devoted to You, and tell everyone the good news of Jesus, the one mediator, who gave Himself for all. Amen.

Questions for reflection

  • Why do you think Paul put prayer for rulers “first of all”?
  • How does Paul’s own story, as a persecutor who was shown mercy, change the way you pray for those who oppose the church?
  • Which leader do you find hardest to pray for? What would you ask God to do for that person?

  • J. C. Ryle, The Upper Room, especially “For Kings”
  • E. M. Bounds, The Essentials of Prayer, especially “The Universality of Prayer”

fields.title: The Prayer Made in Faith
fields.body_html:
“So make it your practice to confess your sins to each other and to pray for each other, so that you may be healed. When a righteous person prays, that prayer is at work, and it can do a great deal.” (James 5:16)

James was one of the men the New Testament calls the brothers of the Lord (Galatians 1:19). Many believe he grew up with Jesus in Nazareth; others, following old traditions, think of him as a stepbrother or a cousin. As we saw in chapter 1, the Lord’s brothers did not believe in Him at first. Then the risen Jesus appeared to James (1 Corinthians 15:7), most likely this James. Everything changed.

Some years later James was a leader of the church in Jerusalem. When the apostles met to decide whether Gentile believers must keep the law of Moses, it was James who stood up at the end and said, “Brothers, listen to what I have to say” (Acts 15:13).

The early Christians remembered James above all as a man of prayer. About a hundred years after his death, a Christian writer named Hegesippus wrote down what was told about him, and the church historian Eusebius copied it into his history of the church. Some details may have grown in the telling, but this picture has been loved for centuries:

“And he was in the habit of entering alone into the temple, and was frequently found upon his knees begging forgiveness for the people, so that his knees became hard like those of a camel, in consequence of his constantly bending them in his worship of God, and asking forgiveness for the people.”

Eusebius, The Church History

The Jewish historian Josephus tells us that James was stoned to death in Jerusalem, around AD 62. The Christian story adds that he knelt as the stones fell and prayed, as Jesus had, “Forgive them, for they know not what they do.”

The church has long believed that this James wrote the letter of James. It is addressed “to the twelve tribes scattered among the nations” (James 1:1), most likely Jewish believers living far from home. Many of them were poor. Rich landowners held back their workers’ pay and dragged believers into court (James 2:6).

At the end of his letter, James turns to prayer. And he begins with the ordinary troubles of life:

“Is any one of you going through hardship? That person should pray. Is anyone in good spirits? That person should sing praises. Is anyone among you ill? That person should call for the elders of the church, and they should pray over the sick person and anoint the sick person with oil in the name of the Lord.” (James 5:13-14)

What James taught about the sick

Imagine a sick believer at home. James says: do not suffer alone. Call for the elders, the leaders of the church, and let them pray over you.

They are to anoint the sick person “with oil in the name of the Lord.” In the ancient world, olive oil was used as a medicine. Oil was also a sign in Scripture of being set apart for God. Christians today understand this anointing in different ways. In some churches it is a sacred rite; in others, elders anoint the sick with a little oil as a simple sign. What matters most is the phrase “in the name of the Lord.” The healing does not come from the oil or from the elders. It comes from the Lord.

Then James promises: “The prayer made in faith will save the one who is ill, and the Lord will raise them up. And if they have committed sins, they will be forgiven” (James 5:15).

Notice the little word “if.” James does not say that every sickness comes from sin. Jesus once told His disciples that a man’s blindness was not caused by his sin or his parents’ sin (John 9:2-3). But sometimes there is sin on our conscience, and sickness can make us face it. So James adds our key verse: confess your sins to each other, and pray for each other. Healing of body and healing of heart belong together.

Elijah, a human being just like us

Then James gives an example from the Old Testament:

“Elijah was a human being just like us. He prayed earnestly that it would not rain, and no rain fell on the land for three years and six months. Then he prayed again, and the sky gave rain and the land produced its crops.” (James 5:17-18)

We may think we could never pray like Elijah. James says he was “just like us.” The same Elijah who prayed on Mount Carmel, with his face between his knees, and sent his servant seven times to look for a cloud (1 Kings 18:42-44), later sat under a broom tree in the wilderness and asked God to let him die (1 Kings 19:4). He was a man who grew tired and afraid. Yet his prayers were at work.

E. M. Bounds loved Elijah, and he saw that the secret was not Elijah’s greatness but his earnestness:

“No sham praying was that of Elijah, no mere performance, no spiritless, soulless, official praying was it. Elijah was in Elijah’s praying. The whole man, with all his fiery forces, was in it.”

E. M. Bounds, Prayer and Praying Men

“A righteous person” in James does not mean a perfect person. It means someone who is right with God through faith, who is honest about sin, and who prays with the whole heart.

When healing does not come

We must be honest. Many faithful believers have called the elders, been anointed, and prayed with great faith, and they were not healed. Some died. Does this mean they did not have enough faith?

The New Testament does not say so. Paul, who healed many, wrote, “I left Trophimus sick in Miletus” (2 Timothy 4:20). Paul himself asked the Lord three times to remove his “thorn in the flesh,” and the Lord answered, “My grace is enough for you” (2 Corinthians 12:7-9). Epaphroditus was spared, and Paul called it God’s mercy (Philippians 2:27).

The prayer made in faith is not faith in our own faith. It is trust in the Lord who “will raise them up.” Sometimes He raises the sick from their beds in this life. Always, for those who belong to Him, He will raise them up on the last day, when He wipes every tear away (Revelation 21:4).

Maria W. Stewart, a Black Christian woman in Boston in the 1800s, sat beside her dying husband. She later wrote about what she cried out to God:

“Spare his life, O God, if consistent with thy will, was my cry; if not, make me to say: ‘Thy will be done.’”

Maria W. Stewart, Meditations from the Pen of Mrs. Maria W. Stewart

Her husband died. But her honest, surrendered prayer was still a prayer of faith. God carried her through her grief and made her a strong voice for her people.

Three key insights

  1. Prayer for the sick is the work of the whole church. James tells the sick to call the elders, and he tells all of us to confess our sins to each other and pray for each other. No one should suffer alone.
  2. The power of prayer comes from God, not from the greatness of the one who prays. Elijah was a human being just like us. A righteous person is not a perfect person, but one who is right with God and prays with the whole heart.
  3. When healing does not come, God has not stopped loving us. Paul left Trophimus sick, and Paul’s own thorn stayed. The prayer made in faith trusts the Lord who will one day raise up all His people and wipe away every tear.

For us today

In many places there is no hospital nearby, and medicine costs more than a family can pay. There, believers often pray for healing with great faith, and God often answers in wonderful ways. Elsewhere, doctors are near, and Christians sometimes forget to pray at all. James calls all of us to bring our sick to the Lord, and he never tells us to refuse medicine. Prayer and doctors are not enemies. Both can be gifts from God.

Be gentle with those who are not healed. Never tell a sick person that they are still ill because their faith is too small. Instead, sit with them, pray with them, and keep praying, as the elders in James did.

And do not forget the first part of our key verse. Many of us carry hidden sins. James invites us to find a trusted brother or sister and confess, so that we can pray for each other and be healed.

Try this

This week, put James 5 into practice.

  • Pray first. When hardship comes this week, stop and pray before you do anything else. When good news comes, sing or speak a word of praise.
  • Visit the sick. Choose one person who is ill, and visit or call them. Ask if you may pray with them.
  • Confess and pray. Find one trusted believer. Share something you are struggling with, and pray for each other.
  • Pray like Elijah. Choose one need and pray for it earnestly every day, as Elijah kept sending his servant to look for the cloud.

A closing prayer

Lord, You are rich in compassion and mercy. I bring You those I love who are sick in body or in mind. Raise them up, Lord, if it is Your will. Where You do not heal, give them Your grace and hold them close. Forgive my sins, and give me the courage to confess them to a brother or sister I can trust. Make me a righteous person whose prayers are at work, not because I am great, but because You are faithful. And keep my hope fixed on the day when You will wipe away every tear. In the name of Jesus. Amen.

Questions for reflection

  • Why do you think James tells the sick to call others, instead of praying alone?
  • How does it encourage you that Elijah was “a human being just like us”?
  • How would you comfort a believer who prayed for healing and was not healed?

  • E. M. Bounds, Purpose in Prayer, especially “Reaching the Ear of God”
  • Maria W. Stewart, Meditations from the Pen of Mrs. Maria W. Stewart, especially “Meditation X”

fields.title: Golden Bowls
fields.body_html:
“Then another angel came, holding a gold censer, and took his place at the altar. Much incense was handed to him, so that he could add it to the prayers of all God’s holy people on the gold altar before the throne. The smoke of the incense rose with the prayers of God’s holy people from the angel’s hand before God.” (Revelation 8:3-4)

Patmos is a small, rocky island in the Aegean Sea, off the coast of what is now Turkey. Near the end of the first century, an old man named John was living there. He tells us why:

“I, John, am your brother, and in Jesus I share with you the affliction, the kingdom, and the endurance. It was because of God’s word and the testimony of Jesus that I came to be on the island called Patmos.” (Revelation 1:9)

Early Christian writers say that this John was the apostle, the last of the Twelve still alive, and that the emperor Domitian had sent him into exile around AD 95. Some think the writer was another John. Either way, he was a prisoner for Christ, far from the churches he loved. By old tradition, Peter and Paul had been put to death years before. James, the brother of the Lord, had been stoned. The churches of Asia were facing pressure and persecution.

Then came the Lord’s day, the first day of the week, when the church met to worship. “On the Lord’s day I came to be in the Spirit,” John writes (Revelation 1:10). And later he saw a door.

“After this I looked, and there in heaven was a door standing open. The voice I had heard at first, the one like a trumpet that spoke with me, said, ‘Come up here, and I will show you what must happen.’” (Revelation 4:1)

Through that door John saw a throne, and Someone seated on it. Around the throne were four living creatures who never stopped worshiping: “Without rest, day and night, they say: ‘Holy, holy, holy, Lord God, the Almighty, the One who was and who is and who is coming’” (Revelation 4:8).

Then John saw a Lamb, “looking as though He had been slaughtered” (Revelation 5:6). It was Jesus, crucified and risen. And as the Lamb took the scroll of God’s plan for history, the living creatures and the elders bowed low before Him:

“Every one of them had a harp, and they held gold bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of God’s holy people.” (Revelation 5:8)

An old man on a lonely island, worshiping on the Lord’s day, was shown that his prayers, and the prayers of every believer on earth, were held in golden bowls before the throne of God.

What John saw

We have seen the first Christians waiting in an upper room, praying under threat, praying for Peter in prison, singing at midnight in Philippi, praying for kings, praying over the sick. Now John lets us see where all those prayers went.

In the temple at Jerusalem, incense was burned on a golden altar every morning and every evening (Exodus 30:7-8), and in chapter 3 we saw God’s people gathering to pray at the hour of the evening offering. The rising smoke was a picture of prayer going up to God. David had prayed, “Let my prayer stand before You like incense” (Psalm 141:2).

In heaven, John sees the true altar of which the temple was only a copy. And the prayers are there. Notice where the bowls of prayer are placed: beside the harps, in the hands of those who worship the Lamb. Our prayers are part of the great worship of heaven.

Notice too who is singing. The new song praises the Lamb because “at the cost of Your blood You bought for God those from every tribe and language and people and nation” (Revelation 5:9). The prayers in the golden bowls are prayed in every language on earth. They come from cathedrals and from huts, from crowded cities and from prison cells.

What the prayers did

In Revelation 8, John sees something even more striking. The Lamb opens the seventh seal, and then:

“When He broke the seventh seal, heaven fell silent for about half an hour.” (Revelation 8:1)

Heaven, which never stops singing, falls silent. Some have thought that heaven goes quiet so that the prayers of the saints may be heard. Then an angel brings the golden censer, adds much incense to “the prayers of all God’s holy people,” and the smoke rises before God. Some Christian teachers have believed that this angel is Christ Himself, our High Priest. Others think he is an angel who serves at the altar.

And then something happens on earth:

“The angel then took the censer, filled it with fire from the altar, and flung it onto the earth. Thunder crashed, there were loud sounds and lightning, and the earth shook.” (Revelation 8:5)

The prayers go up as smoke and come back down as fire. Earlier John had heard the martyrs under the altar cry out, “Holy and true Master, how long until You judge those who live on the earth and give justice for our blood?” (Revelation 6:10). Now heaven answers. The prayers of God’s suffering people are part of how God brings His justice into the world.

Charles Spurgeon pictured heaven waiting in silence, and then the prayers rising:

“Everything is moving now! As soon as the prayers of the saints were mixed with the incense of Christ’s eternal merit and begun to smoke up from the altar, then prayer became effectual!”

Charles H. Spurgeon, Mighty Power in Prayer

“Effectual” means that the prayer does its work. The weak prayers of a persecuted church are not wasted words. They move heaven, and heaven moves the earth.

Samuel Rutherford, a Scottish pastor of the 1600s who was himself banished from his church for a time, gave this advice to a friend who felt his prayers were too poor to matter:

“I shall rather spill twenty prayers, than not pray at all. Let my broken words go up to heaven: when they come up into the Great Angel’s golden censer, that compassionate Advocate will put together my broken prayers, and perfume them.”

Samuel Rutherford, Letters of Samuel Rutherford

“Come, Lord Jesus”

The book of Revelation ends with a prayer. Jesus speaks: “Yes, I am coming soon!” And John answers for the whole church: “Amen! Come, Lord Jesus!” (Revelation 22:20).

This was one of the first prayers of the church. Paul ends his first letter to the Corinthians with the words, “Our Lord, come!” (1 Corinthians 16:22). In the Greek of his letter he kept an Aramaic phrase, Marana tha, probably the words the first believers in Jerusalem had prayed in their own language. From the upper room to Patmos, the church kept praying it. The Spirit and the bride, which is the church, say, “Come!” (Revelation 22:17).

All the prayers in the golden bowls lean toward that day. Every prayer for healing looks ahead to the day when there will be “no more mourning, no crying, no pain” (Revelation 21:4). Every prayer for justice looks ahead to the day when the Lamb reigns. Every prayer for the lost looks ahead to the great crowd “from every nation and from all tribes and peoples and languages” standing before the throne (Revelation 7:9).

Three key insights

  1. Our prayers are part of the worship of heaven. John saw the prayers of God’s people held in golden bowls beside the harps of those who worship the Lamb. When we pray on earth, we join the song of heaven.
  2. The prayers of God’s people move heaven, and heaven moves the earth. The prayers rose as smoke before God and came back to earth as fire. God has chosen to work His purposes in the world in answer to the prayers of His people.
  3. Every prayer leans toward the coming of Jesus. The last prayer of the Bible is “Come, Lord Jesus!” All our prayers for healing, justice and salvation look ahead to the day when He returns and makes all things new.

For us today

John was old, alone and in exile when heaven’s door opened. You may be old, or alone, or far from home. You may be in a prison, a hospital, a refugee camp, or a home where no one else prays. You may feel that your prayers are too weak to matter. John’s vision tells you that heaven holds them in golden bowls.

When you pray, picture the throne. Believers in Nigeria, India, Brazil, Korea, China, Egypt and every other land are praying too, in hundreds of languages, and every one of those prayers rises before God like incense.

When you see war, injustice and persecution, do not lose heart. Heaven is listening, and the Lamb is on the throne.

Try this

This week, let John’s vision shape your prayers.

  • Read heaven’s worship. Read Revelation 4 and 5 slowly each day. Picture the throne and the golden bowls.
  • Begin with praise. Before you ask for anything, join the song: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God, the Almighty.”
  • Pray with the nations. Each day, choose one country and pray for the believers there. Picture their prayers and yours rising together before the throne.
  • End with “Come.” Close each prayer this week with the oldest prayer of the church: “Come, Lord Jesus.”

A closing prayer

Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty, You are seated on the throne, and the Lamb who was slain is worthy of all praise. Thank You that my prayers are not lost. Thank You that You hold them in golden bowls, with the prayers of Your people from every tribe and language and nation. Take my weak and broken words and make them rise before You like incense. Hear the cries of Your suffering people, and bring Your justice to the earth. Keep me praying until the day I see You face to face. Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!

Questions for reflection

  • How does it change your prayers to know that they are part of the worship of heaven?
  • John received his vision while he was in exile and praying alone. When have you found God near in a lonely place?
  • What do you long for most when you pray, “Come, Lord Jesus”?

Read more on Ochorus

  • E. M. Bounds, The Reality of Prayer, especially “God Has Everything to Do with Prayer”
  • Samuel Rutherford, Letters of Samuel Rutherford, especially “Letter CCXCIII: To Mr. James Wilson”
  • Thomas Watson, A Body of Divinity, especially “Christ’s Priestly Office”

fields.title: Conclusion: Passing the Torch
fields.body_html:
“Keep in mind those who led you, who brought you the word of God. Look closely at where their way of life led them, and follow the example of their faith.” (Hebrews 13:7)

The book of Acts ends in an unexpected way. Paul is in Rome, under guard, waiting for his trial before the emperor. We are not told how the trial ended or how Paul died. Luke simply leaves him in a rented room, welcoming everyone who came, where “he proclaimed the kingdom of God and taught the things about the Lord Jesus Christ, with all boldness, unhindered” (Acts 28:31).

It is as if Luke put down his pen in the middle of the story on purpose. The story of the praying church was not finished. It was only beginning.

In this book we have followed that story from an upstairs room in Jerusalem to a prison in Philippi and a rented room in Rome, and finally to John on the island of Patmos, watching the prayers of God’s people rise like incense before the throne. Some sixty years before, the first believers had been a hundred and twenty people in one room. By the time John wrote, there were churches across the Roman world, from Jerusalem to Rome, and Christians who prayed in Aramaic, Greek and Latin.

What the first church taught us

Here, in a few lines, is some of what the first believers have taught us about prayer:

  • Waiting on God is not wasted time, and prayer makes one family out of very different people (chapter 1).
  • Prayer was one of the four things the first church would not let go (chapter 2).
  • Set times of prayer help us keep praying, and teach us to see the people others pass by (chapter 3).
  • Begin with who God is, and ask for boldness rather than safety (chapter 4).
  • Prayer is real work, and it needs protected time (chapter 5).
  • Praying for our enemies is the clearest sign of forgiveness (chapter 6).
  • God remembers every sincere prayer (chapter 7).
  • The church’s first and strongest response to danger is prayer, and God answers even prayers mixed with doubt (chapter 8).
  • God often guides His people while they are worshiping Him and fasting (chapter 9).
  • A small prayer meeting by a river can be the beginning of a great work (chapter 10).
  • Praise can rise from the darkest place (chapter 11).
  • The greatest thing we can ask for anyone is that they would know God better (chapter 12).
  • God is able to do far beyond anything we ask or think (chapter 13).
  • When we do not know what to pray, the Spirit prays for us (chapter 14).
  • When we cannot be with the people we love, we can still fight for them in prayer (chapter 15).
  • Worry is a signal to pray, and God’s peace can guard us before anything changes (chapter 16).
  • Praying without stopping is for ordinary working people (chapter 17).
  • Prayer for those in power comes first, not last, even for rulers who persecute (chapter 18).
  • Prayer for the sick is the work of the whole church, and God’s love holds when healing does not come (chapter 19).
  • Our prayers are part of the worship of heaven, and every prayer leans toward the coming of Jesus (chapter 20).

You will find every one of these lessons gathered by theme in Appendix 1, and every Scripture in this book listed in Bible order in Appendix 2.

Ordinary people who prayed

Look back over the people in this book. Fishermen and tax collectors. Widows who needed food. A Roman army officer. A servant girl named Rhoda who forgot to open the door. A businesswoman by a river. A jailer who had locked up two preachers and then washed their wounds. A man named Epaphras whose name we would not know if Paul had not mentioned his prayers.

The leaders of Jerusalem were astonished at Peter and John, because “they realized these were men without formal schooling, just ordinary people,” and “they recognized that the two had been companions of Jesus” (Acts 4:13). That is the secret of the first church. They were not great people. They had been with Jesus, and they kept on being with Him in prayer.

They did not have church buildings, printed Bibles or books about prayer. Many of them could not read. Some of them were slaves. Many suffered for their faith, and some died for it. And yet, within a single lifetime, the good news had traveled from Jerusalem to the capital of the empire. Underneath it all, again and again, Luke writes the same words: they prayed.

The torch is passed

The letter to the Hebrews tells its readers to remember those who led them, and to “follow the example of their faith” (Hebrews 13:7). That is what the next generation of Christians did.

In Volume 4, Faithful unto Death, we will meet them. We will read the Didache, one of the oldest Christian writings outside the New Testament, which taught believers to pray the Lord’s Prayer three times a day. We will hear Clement of Rome praying for the rulers who persecuted the church, and Ignatius praying on his way to the lions. We will stand with old Polycarp as he prays before the fire, and with Perpetua in her prison cell. We will follow Antony into the desert and listen to the desert mothers and fathers. We will hear Monica weeping for her son Augustine, and Augustine himself confessing that our hearts are restless until they rest in God. And we will learn, with the monks of the East, to pray, “Lord Jesus Christ, have mercy.”

They were the children and grandchildren of the church in Acts. They prayed as they had been taught, often under the threat of death, and the church kept growing.

Your turn

The church in Acts did not end with the last chapter of Acts. It goes on wherever believers pray. You are part of it.

So gather with others to pray, as the hundred and twenty did. Keep set times of prayer, as Peter and John did. When you are threatened, begin with who God is. When you are wronged, pray for those who wrong you. When you are in prison, real or otherwise, sing. Pray for your leaders, for the sick, for the missionaries far away and the neighbors nearby. When you do not know what to pray, let the Spirit help you. And when you cannot see any answer at all, remember the golden bowls. Not one of your prayers is lost.

The writer of Hebrews said it best: since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, “let us keep our eyes on Jesus” (Hebrews 12:2). He is the one the first church prayed to, the one they prayed in the name of, and the one who prays for us still.

A closing prayer

Sovereign Master, maker of heaven and earth, thank You for the first church, for its courage and its prayers. Thank You for the hundred and twenty in the upper room, for Stephen who prayed for his killers, for the church that prayed through the night for Peter, for Paul and Silas singing at midnight, and for every ordinary believer whose prayers built Your church. Make me devoted to prayer as they were. Fill me with Your Holy Spirit. Give me boldness to speak and love to pray for others, even my enemies. Keep me faithful to the end, and let my prayers rise before You with all Your holy people, until Jesus comes. Come, Lord Jesus. Amen.

fields.title: Appendix 1: Key Insights
fields.body_html:
Every chapter of this book closes with three key insights. Here they are gathered by theme, each pointing back to the chapter where it is taught and to that chapter’s key verse.

The Father’s Love

  • God remembers every sincere prayer. Chapter 7, Prayers That Rose Before God (Acts 10:4)
  • God is never too busy for His children. Chapter 17, Never Stop Praying (1 Thessalonians 5:16-18)

Learning to Pray

  • Scripture gives us words when we are afraid. Chapter 4, “Sovereign Master”: Praying Under Threat (Acts 4:31)
  • Not knowing what to pray is not a failure; it is where the Spirit’s help begins. Chapter 14, When We Do Not Know What to Pray (Romans 8:26)

Making Room for Prayer

  • Prayer was one of the four things the first church would not let go. Chapter 2, Devoted to the Prayers (Acts 2:42)
  • Set times of prayer help us keep praying. Chapter 3, The Hour of Prayer (Acts 3:1)
  • Prayer is real work, and it needs protected time. Chapter 5, Holding Fast to Prayer (Acts 6:4)
  • Good work can crowd out prayer as easily as bad work. Chapter 5, Holding Fast to Prayer (Acts 6:4)
  • Fasting is prayer with the whole person. Chapter 9, Worship, Fasting and Sending (Acts 13:2-3)
  • God loves to meet people at the places where they faithfully pray. Chapter 10, The Place of Prayer by the River (Acts 16:13)
  • Praying without stopping is for ordinary working people. Chapter 17, Never Stop Praying (1 Thessalonians 5:16-18)

Asking Boldly

  • God is able to do far beyond anything we ask or think. Chapter 13, Rooted Deep in Love (Ephesians 3:16-19)
  • The prayers of God’s people move heaven, and heaven moves the earth. Chapter 20, Golden Bowls (Revelation 8:3-4)

Persistence

  • Waiting on God is not wasted time. Chapter 1, Waiting in the Upper Room (Acts 1:14)
  • A great day of blessing must be followed by daily prayer. Chapter 2, Devoted to the Prayers (Acts 2:42)
  • Prayer for others is often hard, and that is no sign that it is wrong. Chapter 15, Always Wrestling in Prayer (Colossians 4:12)

Faith

  • We can give others only what we have first received from God. Chapter 3, The Hour of Prayer (Acts 3:1)
  • Begin with who God is before you speak about the danger. Chapter 4, “Sovereign Master”: Praying Under Threat (Acts 4:31)
  • God answers even prayers mixed with doubt. Chapter 8, Peter in Prison, the Church on Its Knees (Acts 12:5)
  • Only the Lord can open a heart. Chapter 10, The Place of Prayer by the River (Acts 16:13)
  • The power that raised Jesus from the dead is at work for those who believe. Chapter 12, That You May Know Him Better (Ephesians 1:16-19)
  • The power of prayer comes from God, not from the greatness of the one who prays. Chapter 19, The Prayer Made in Faith (James 5:16)
  • Every prayer leans toward the coming of Jesus. Chapter 20, Golden Bowls (Revelation 8:3-4)

Humility and Mercy

  • Prayer changes the one who prays. Chapter 7, Prayers That Rose Before God (Acts 10:4)
  • God wants rulers to be saved, even the ones who persecute. Chapter 18, For Kings and All in Authority (1 Timothy 2:1-2)

Forgiveness

  • Praying for our enemies is the clearest sign of forgiveness. Chapter 6, “Do Not Charge Them with This Sin” (Acts 7:60)

Thanksgiving

  • Praise can rise from the darkest place. Chapter 11, Songs at Midnight (Acts 16:25)
  • Paul’s prayers begin with thanks for what God has already done. Chapter 12, That You May Know Him Better (Ephesians 1:16-19)
  • Thanksgiving belongs inside every request. Chapter 16, Do Not Worry About Anything (Philippians 4:6-7)
  • Joy, prayer and thanks belong together. Chapter 17, Never Stop Praying (1 Thessalonians 5:16-18)

Guidance and Surrender

  • The first church placed its first decision in God’s hands. Chapter 1, Waiting in the Upper Room (Acts 1:14)
  • God often answers one person’s prayer through another person’s prayer. Chapter 7, Prayers That Rose Before God (Acts 10:4)
  • God often guides His people while they are worshiping Him. Chapter 9, Worship, Fasting and Sending (Acts 13:2-3)
  • The Spirit always prays in line with what God wants. Chapter 14, When We Do Not Know What to Pray (Romans 8:26)
  • The best prayer for others asks that they will stand firm and grow mature in God’s will. Chapter 15, Always Wrestling in Prayer (Colossians 4:12)
  • God’s peace can guard us before our circumstances change. Chapter 16, Do Not Worry About Anything (Philippians 4:6-7)

Prayer in Suffering and Testing

  • The first church asked for boldness, not for safety. Chapter 4, “Sovereign Master”: Praying Under Threat (Acts 4:31)
  • We learn to pray in hard times by watching how Jesus prayed. Chapter 6, “Do Not Charge Them with This Sin” (Acts 7:60)
  • God’s different answers are not a measure of our faith. Chapter 8, Peter in Prison, the Church on Its Knees (Acts 12:5)
  • God’s purpose in our trouble may be bigger than our escape. Chapter 11, Songs at Midnight (Acts 16:25)
  • Paul asks first for strength on the inside, not for an easier life on the outside. Chapter 13, Rooted Deep in Love (Ephesians 3:16-19)
  • Worry is a signal to pray, not a secret to hide. Chapter 16, Do Not Worry About Anything (Philippians 4:6-7)
  • We can pray for a ruler without approving of evil. Chapter 18, For Kings and All in Authority (1 Timothy 2:1-2)
  • When healing does not come, God has not stopped loving us. Chapter 19, The Prayer Made in Faith (James 5:16)

Praying Together

  • Prayer made one family out of very different people. Chapter 1, Waiting in the Upper Room (Acts 1:14)
  • The first church prayed together, in the temple and at home. Chapter 2, Devoted to the Prayers (Acts 2:42)
  • The church’s first and strongest response to danger is prayer. Chapter 8, Peter in Prison, the Church on Its Knees (Acts 12:5)
  • A small prayer meeting can be the beginning of a great work. Chapter 10, The Place of Prayer by the River (Acts 16:13)
  • It is a gift to have someone to pray with in the dark. Chapter 11, Songs at Midnight (Acts 16:25)
  • We learn the love of Christ together with all God’s holy people. Chapter 13, Rooted Deep in Love (Ephesians 3:16-19)
  • Prayer for the sick is the work of the whole church. Chapter 19, The Prayer Made in Faith (James 5:16)
  • Our prayers are part of the worship of heaven. Chapter 20, Golden Bowls (Revelation 8:3-4)

Praying for Others

  • Praying people learn to see the people others pass by. Chapter 3, The Hour of Prayer (Acts 3:1)
  • When God’s people share the load, their leaders are free to pray for them. Chapter 5, Holding Fast to Prayer (Acts 6:4)
  • God may answer our prayers long after we are gone. Chapter 6, “Do Not Charge Them with This Sin” (Acts 7:60)
  • Every believer can share in mission by praying and sending. Chapter 9, Worship, Fasting and Sending (Acts 13:2-3)
  • The greatest thing we can ask for anyone is that they would know God better. Chapter 12, That You May Know Him Better (Ephesians 1:16-19)
  • When we cannot be with the people we love, we can still fight for them in prayer. Chapter 15, Always Wrestling in Prayer (Colossians 4:12)
  • Prayer for those in power comes first, not last. Chapter 18, For Kings and All in Authority (1 Timothy 2:1-2)

Christ Who Prays for Us

  • The Holy Spirit prays for us, and the Son prays for us too. Chapter 14, When We Do Not Know What to Pray (Romans 8:26)
